title: Napoleon Dynamite
logline: An awkward Idaho teen helps his friend run for class president. Deadpan, awkward-pause comedy.
overview: A listless and alienated teenager decides to help his new friend win the class presidency in their small western high school, while he must deal with his bizarre family life back home.
tagline: He's out to prove he's got nothing to prove.

jokes.text: 'What are you gonna do today, Napoleon?' / 'Whatever I feel like I want to do. Gosh!'
jokes.setup: Grandma asks a mundane, caring question about Napoleon's plans for the day
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's response — 'Whatever I feel like I want to do. Gosh!' — is an absurdly defensive non-answer delivered with maximum irritation, as if the question was an insufferable imposition
jokes.explanation: This is the film's first real joke and it's a perfect character introduction. The disproportionate irritation Napoleon shows toward a totally reasonable question instantly communicates everything about him. 'Gosh!' as a mild expletive is funny in itself — it's the fury of a teenager channeled through a word a child would use. The economy is exceptional. Scores high because it's character-defining, quotable, and works better on rewatch when you know Napoleon's full personality.

jokes.text: Napoleon's current events report: Japanese scientists 'explaced' — placed — explosive detonators at the bottom of Lake Loch Ness to blow Nessie out of the water
jokes.setup: Napoleon is called on to give a current events report, a mundane school assignment
jokes.punchline: He self-corrects his malapropism mid-sentence ('explaced — placed') and then proceeds to describe a completely fabricated, deranged news story about blowing up the Loch Ness Monster with explosives as though it were a real news item
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The self-corrected malapropism ('explaced — placed') is a perfect deadpan detail — he notices the error and fixes it without breaking stride, as if the rest of what he's saying is completely credible. The escalation into 'Scotland's local wizards casting a protective spell' and 'our underwater ally' transforms a school assignment into a window into Napoleon's deeply weird inner world. The utter confidence of the delivery is the engine of the comedy. Genuinely original — this joke could only come from this character.

jokes.text: Napoleon continues: 'Sir Curt Godfrey of the Nessie Alliance summoned the help of Scotland's local wizards to cast a protective spell over the lake and its local residents'
jokes.setup: Napoleon's already absurd Loch Ness report continues with the introduction of an opposing faction
jokes.punchline: 'Scotland's local wizards' casting a protective spell — the report escalates from pseudo-scientific (explosives) to pure fantasy (wizards) with no acknowledgment of the tonal leap
jokes.explanation: The escalation from explosive detonators to wizards is the comedic peak of the Loch Ness bit. The joke works because Napoleon's deadpan commitment never wavers — 'Scotland's local wizards' is delivered with the same gravity as a real news report. The title 'Sir Curt Godfrey of the Nessie Alliance' is also funny as specific invented bureaucracy. This beat extends joke #2 but earns its own entry as a distinct escalation.

jokes.text: '...and all those who seek for the peaceful existence of our underwater ally.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon's current events report has described wizards casting spells over Loch Ness
jokes.punchline: He closes the report with 'our underwater ally' — treating the Loch Ness Monster as a recognized diplomatic partner of unspecified nations, delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: 'Our underwater ally' is a perfect button on the Loch Ness bit. The word 'ally' implies geopolitical alliance — Nessie as a recognized nation-state partner — which is the culmination of Napoleon presenting total fantasy as journalism. Economy is very high: three words do enormous absurdist work.

jokes.text: Teacher's reaction after Napoleon finishes: 'Yes. Yes.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon has just delivered an insane current events report about Loch Ness wizards
jokes.punchline: The teacher's response is a flat, resigned 'Yes. Yes.' — not correcting him, not engaging with the absurdity, just moving on. The audience imagines the teacher's dead-eyed acceptance
jokes.explanation: The teacher's non-reaction is the perfect payoff to the Loch Ness sequence. 'Yes. Yes.' is economy at its finest — it implies the teacher has given up, that this is routine, and that no one will challenge Napoleon's reality. The understated acceptance is funnier than any correction or outrage would be.

jokes.text: 'I told you. I spent it with my uncle in Alaska hunting wolverines.' / 'Did you shoot any?' / 'Yes, like 50 of 'em. They kept tryin' to attack my cousins. What the heck would you do in a situation like that?'
jokes.setup: A classmate asks what Napoleon did last summer, implying they've had this conversation before ('I told you')
jokes.punchline: Napoleon claims to have shot 50 wolverines in Alaska, and then rhetorically challenges the classmate — 'What the heck would you do in a situation like that?' — as if this is a completely plausible and relatable scenario
jokes.explanation: Napoleon's tall tales are a core character comedy mechanism. '50 of 'em' is a great specific number — not 'a bunch,' but 50, implying he kept count. The rhetorical 'What the heck would you do?' is the kicker — he's genuinely puzzled anyone would question this. The defensiveness confirms he's lying while his confidence says he believes it. Pure Napoleon character comedy.

jokes.text: 'What kind of gun did you use?' / 'A frickin' 12-gauge. What do you think?'
jokes.setup: Classmate asks a follow-up question about Napoleon's wolverine hunting story
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's 'A frickin' 12-gauge. What do you think?' treats the question as insulting — as if the answer were obvious — while his mild profanity ('frickin'') mirrors the 'Gosh!' energy: big attitude, neutered language
jokes.explanation: The 'frickin' + 'What do you think?' combo establishes Napoleon's voice — maximum irritation through minimum vocabulary. Good character work, slightly lower originality than the first appearances of this pattern.

jokes.text: A bigger kid threatens Napoleon: 'You think you're funny? You just watch your step.' Napoleon says 'But I didn't—' and trail off
jokes.setup: Napoleon's tall tale has apparently annoyed or impressed a bigger kid nearby
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's threat-receiving reaction — 'But I didn't—' — is a helpless, unfinished protest. He can't even complete a defense. The bully's completely disproportionate aggression to Napoleon just telling a story is absurd
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — Napoleon is victimized by someone who doesn't even have a good reason. The unfinished 'But I didn't—' is a nice deadpan detail. Not a standout moment but serves the film's consistent tone of Napoleon being perpetually put-upon.

jokes.text: 'Can you bring me my Chap Stick?' / 'No, Napoleon.' / 'But my lips hurt real bad.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon calls home claiming to feel sick and asks his brother Kip to come get him; Kip refuses
jokes.punchline: Napoleon pivots to asking for Chap Stick, and when denied, insists 'But my lips hurt real bad' — escalating his suffering to this mundane, minuscule complaint with utter sincerity
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable moments in the entire film and arguably the best joke in this reel. The structure is flawless: Napoleon escalates from a legitimate sick-day request to 'just come get me' to the trivial Chap Stick ask, and then the punchline — 'But my lips hurt real bad' — is delivered with the same gravity as a terminal diagnosis. The bathos is perfect. It's character-defining: Napoleon's self-pity is indistinguishable from genuine crisis in his own mind. Scores near 9 on craft because the economy and character integration are both exceptional, and 'my lips hurt real bad' has become a genuine cultural touchstone quote from this film.

jokes.text: Napoleon's response to being told to borrow ChapStick from the nurse: 'I'm not gonna use hers, you sicko.'
jokes.setup: Kip tells Napoleon to just borrow ChapStick from the school nurse who has five sticks in her drawer
jokes.punchline: Napoleon refuses in disgust and calls Kip a 'sicko' — the hygienic objection to sharing ChapStick is treated as a profound moral failing on Kip's part, while Napoleon's own behavior is never rational
jokes.explanation: 'You sicko' is a great button on the ChapStick sequence. Napoleon's self-righteousness about the nurse's ChapStick while simultaneously suffering from desperately chapped lips is a perfect internal contradiction. The word 'sicko' — again, mild vocabulary for large outrage — is very on-brand. Good payoff to joke #9.

jokes.text: 'You know, there's, like, a buttload of gangs at this school. This one gang kept wanting me to join 'cause I'm pretty good with a bow staff.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon is showing new student Pedro around the school as a welcoming gesture
jokes.punchline: His opening conversational gambit is an unprompted warning about gangs, followed immediately by a boast about his bow staff skills as the reason gangs recruit him — presented as casual, normal orientation information
jokes.explanation: This is a top-tier joke in the reel. The 'bow staff' boast is Napoleon's character in miniature: the tall tale, the specific obscure skill, the total social obliviousness to how this sounds, and the casual insertion of gang recruitment as an everyday school orientation fact. It's also the introduction of Pedro, and Napoleon's attempt to impress him with dangerous-sounding nonsense is perfect first-impression comedy. 'Buttload' as a quantifier is also very Napoleon. The character integration is as high as it gets — no other character in film history would say this.

jokes.text: 'What kind of bike do you have?' / 'It's a Sledgehammer.' / 'Dang! You got shocks, pegs. Lucky!'
jokes.setup: Napoleon asks Pedro what kind of bike he rides to school
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's breathless, genuine admiration for Pedro's bike — 'Dang! You got shocks, pegs. Lucky!' — is the response of someone who finds this mundane information genuinely impressive and exciting
jokes.explanation: 'Dang! You got shocks, pegs. Lucky!' is a great character moment — Napoleon's authentic, childlike excitement about basic bike features reveals his social world. The sentence fragments and exclamatory delivery make it very quotable. 'Lucky!' as a final, envious punctuation is perfect. Works because it's sincere rather than ironic.

jokes.text: 'You ever take it off any sweet jumps?'
jokes.setup: Napoleon has just admired Pedro's bike and they are apparently now riding it
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's question — 'You ever take it off any sweet jumps?' — is delivered as a serious, knowing inquiry from one extreme sports enthusiast to another, despite Napoleon being the least extreme-sports person imaginable
jokes.explanation: 'Sweet jumps' is a highly quotable phrase that became associated with the film. Napoleon's sincere use of extreme-sports vocabulary is funny because of the gap between his aspirational vocabulary and his reality. The economy is excellent — four words do a lot of character work.

jokes.text: 'You got, like, three feet of air that time.' — Napoleon watching/commenting while Pedro rides
jokes.setup: Napoleon asked Pedro about sweet jumps; Pedro apparently attempts one on his bike
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's color commentary — 'You got, like, three feet of air that time' — delivered as serious expert analysis, implies whatever Pedro did was much less impressive than three feet of air. The gap between Napoleon's breathless commentary and the presumably modest reality is the joke
jokes.explanation: Continuation of the sweet jumps bit. Napoleon's instant expert assessment is funny, particularly the 'like' hedge undermining the false precision of 'three feet.' Slight diminishing returns from joke #13 but still a good beat.

jokes.text: 'Can I try it really quick?' — Napoleon asks to try Pedro's bike
jokes.setup: Napoleon has been enthusiastically coaching Pedro on his bike and praising his jump
jokes.punchline: Napoleon immediately asks to try it himself — the comedic payoff being the anticipated (and apparently delivered) spectacle of Napoleon attempting a 'sweet jump' on a bike
jokes.explanation: The setup for a visual gag — Napoleon presumably crashes or makes a poor attempt. The 'really quick' qualifier is a nice Napoleon-ism, as if he won't take long. Gets the rewatch bonus because viewers anticipate what's coming.

jokes.text: Napoleon apparently crashes Pedro's bike; someone yells 'Taint!'
jokes.setup: Napoleon asked to try Pedro's bike and attempt a sweet jump
jokes.punchline: The implied crash/failure, punctuated by someone shouting 'Taint!' — a rude exclamation that's funny both as a reaction and as a mild profanity Napoleon-universe substitute
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the sweet jumps sequence. Without seeing the visual, the transcript gives us 'Taint!' as a reaction which implies something went badly. The physical comedy here depends heavily on the visual; the transcript alone gives only partial credit. Functional escalation payoff.

jokes.text: Napoleon's internal monologue/poem about a girl: 'I love the way your sandy hair floats in the air / To me it's like a lullaby / I'm just flying by, oh so high / like a kite tied to a stake.'
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of the bike crash, Napoleon apparently sees an attractive girl and his inner romantic voice emerges
jokes.punchline: 'Like a kite tied to a stake' — the poem starts as passable romantic-teen sentiment and then ends on a deeply odd, contradictory image: a kite that cannot fly because it's staked to the ground. The failed metaphor delivered with Napoleon's earnestness is the joke
jokes.explanation: This is a quietly brilliant joke. The poem tracks as genuine adolescent romantic poetry until the final image — 'like a kite tied to a stake' — which is a perfect metaphor for nothing. A kite tied to a stake doesn't fly; it's the opposite of the transcendence Napoleon is reaching for. Whether intentional on Napoleon's part or not, the image reveals his stunted emotional vocabulary. It's the most literary joke in the reel and deeply character-integrated. High originality because this specific joke construction — sincere bad poetry with a catastrophically wrong closing metaphor — is unusual in film comedy.

jokes.text: 'How was school?' / 'The worst day of my life. What do you think?'
jokes.setup: Grandma greets Napoleon after school with a standard parental question
jokes.punchline: 'The worst day of my life. What do you think?' — Napoleon treats a routine school day as a catastrophe, and the 'What do you think?' mirrors his opening 'What do you think?' energy: disproportionate exasperation at being asked anything
jokes.explanation: Napoleon's interaction with Grandma is a running dynamic — she asks reasonable questions, he treats them as profound violations. 'The worst day of my life' for a school day he spent telling tall tales and hanging out with a new friend is perfect. The 'What do you think?' appendage is very Napoleon. Slightly lower originality than the first instance of this pattern.

jokes.text: 'Kip hasn't done flipping anything today.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon is complaining about his day; Grandma is talking about going out
jokes.punchline: Napoleon gratuitously throws Kip under the bus — 'Kip hasn't done flipping anything today' — apropos of nothing, as a mid-complaint aside. 'Flipping' as a mild expletive is consistent with Napoleon's vocabulary register
jokes.explanation: Minor joke. Napoleon's unprompted fraternal tattling is a character beat — he's the kind of person who complains about others' laziness while doing nothing himself. 'Flipping' continues the mild-expletive pattern. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Grandma: 'Knock it off, Napoleon. Make yourself a dang quesadilla!'
jokes.setup: Napoleon whines about there being nothing to eat when Grandma announces she's leaving for the night
jokes.punchline: 'Make yourself a dang quesadilla!' — Grandma gives as good as she gets. The word 'dang' mirrors the household's shared vocabulary of mild expletives, and the specificity of 'quesadilla' as the offered solution is funny
jokes.explanation: Very quotable line. The specificity of 'quesadilla' — not 'make yourself something' but a specific food — is funny. 'Dang' in Grandma's mouth confirms this is a shared family dialect. Good character work showing Grandma isn't a pushover despite Napoleon's complaints.

jokes.text: 'Napoleon, don't be jealous that I've been chatting online with babes all day. Besides, we both know I'm training to become a cage fighter.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon tells Kip to stay home and eat chips (mocking him); Kip responds
jokes.punchline: Kip's response is a masterpiece of delusional self-image: (1) he's been chatting with 'babes' online all day, (2) he's training to be a cage fighter — both claims delivered with total sincerity by a visibly unimpressive adult man who lives with his grandmother
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. Kip is introduced here as a full comic creation: a grown man living at home, achieving nothing, who nevertheless narrates his life as a series of impressive achievements. 'Don't be jealous' implies Napoleon should envy him — which is absurd. 'We both know I'm training to become a cage fighter' positions this as shared, established fact — a beautiful piece of delusional character logic. The two claims together (online babes + cage fighting) are perfectly paired escalations. Character integration is near-maximum: this joke could only come from Kip.

jokes.text: 'Since when, Kip? You have the worst reflexes of all time.'
jokes.setup: Kip claims he's training to become a cage fighter
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's instant, deadpan takedown: 'You have the worst reflexes of all time' — not 'bad reflexes' but 'worst of all time,' which is a quintessentially Napoleon hyperbolic superlative
jokes.explanation: 'Worst of all time' is a Napoleon superlative — the same logic as 'worst day of my life.' Here it functions as a devastating comeback. The irony is Napoleon saying this while being himself fairly useless. Good economy, good structure.

jokes.text: 'Try and hit me, Napoleon.' / 'What?' / 'I said come down here and see what happens if you try and hit me.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon calls out Kip's reflexes; Kip, committed to his cage-fighter identity, issues a challenge
jokes.punchline: Kip's challenge — 'come down here and see what happens if you try and hit me' — is delivered by a man who has just admitted to spending the day chatting online and who lives with his grandmother. The gap between his threat and his reality is the joke
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Kip's cage-fighter delusion into an actual confrontation challenge is good character comedy. The 'What?' from Napoleon — genuine confusion that Kip would say this — is a great reaction. We know Kip cannot fight. The anticipation of Kip being immediately proven wrong is the comedic tension.

jokes.text: Napoleon attempts to hit Kip; the attempt is apparently feeble: 'Such an idiot. Let me see what your best move is.'
jokes.setup: Kip dared Napoleon to try and hit him; Napoleon apparently tries
jokes.punchline: Kip's response — 'Such an idiot. Let me see what your best move is' — implies Napoleon's attempt was so bad it barely registered, and now Kip is pivoting to offense. Both of them fighting is the joke: two incompetent people pretending to fight seriously
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the cage-fighter setup. The visual of Napoleon and Kip feebly attempting to fight in their grandmother's house is funny; the transcript's 'Geez!' reaction (joke #25) confirms Napoleon eventually gets got. This beat is primarily visual comedy that the transcript hints at.

jokes.text: 'I'll go get it. Geez!' — Napoleon after apparently getting hit or seeing something from Kip
jokes.setup: Kip wants to show Napoleon his 'best move'
jokes.punchline: 'Geez!' — Napoleon's reaction after Kip apparently makes contact or demonstrates something unexpectedly effective. The payoff is that Kip's 'training' may have produced at least one functional move
jokes.explanation: Button on the cage-fighter sequence. 'Geez!' as Napoleon's mild exclamation of surprise/pain is funny in context — Kip actually managed something. Without the visual it's harder to fully score. Functional payoff.

jokes.text: Deb's door-to-door glamour shots pitch: 'Um, hello. Would you like to look like this?' [holds up photo] 'This is a girl.' — Napoleon's reaction to the photo
jokes.setup: A girl (Deb) shows up at the door selling glamour shots and holds up a photo as an example of the results
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's flat clarification — 'This is a girl' — implies the glamour shot is so unflattering or ambiguous that gender identification is necessary, delivered completely without malice or irony, just as a neutral observation
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous laugh. Napoleon's correction is not unkind — he's just processing the information and finding it needs clarification. The deadpan delivery makes it work: he's not mocking Deb, he's just literally confused. The economy (9.5) is near-perfect — 'This is a girl' is as economical as a joke can be. Scores high because the gap between Deb's sales pitch and Napoleon's flat incomprehension is very funny, and the specific three-word response is exactly right.

jokes.text: 'I already get my hair cut at the Cuttin' Corral.'
jokes.setup: Deb pitches glamour shots as a beauty service Napoleon might want
jokes.punchline: Napoleon declines by citing his existing hair arrangement — the 'Cuttin' Corral,' a name that evokes a low-budget, western-themed small-town barbershop — as though this is a reasonable competing luxury service
jokes.explanation: The 'Cuttin' Corral' is funny primarily as a piece of Idaho world-building — it's the perfect name for a haircut place in this town. Napoleon's matter-of-fact citation of it as a luxury competitor to glamour shots is good character work. The name 'Cuttin' Corral' does most of the comedic lifting.

jokes.text: Because for a limited time only, glamour shots by Deb are 75% off.
jokes.setup: Deb is pitching her glamour shots business door-to-door.
jokes.punchline: The 75% off — not 10%, not half price, but 75% off — implies her glamour shots are either catastrophically failing to sell at full price, or the full price was so high that 75% off is still accessible. The businesslike pitch from someone who is clearly not a professional makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Minor beat within the Deb sequence but the specificity of 75% — suggesting either desperation or wild overconfidence — adds texture to Deb's character as a small-town entrepreneur going door to door.

jokes.text: Rex Kwon Do infomercial interrupts: 'I'm Rex, founder of the Rex Kwon Do Self-Defense System. After one week with me in my dojo, you'll be prepared to defend yourself with the strength of a grizzly, the reflexes of a puma, and the wisdom of a man.'
jokes.setup: In what appears to be a TV commercial playing in the background, Rex introduces his self-defense system
jokes.punchline: 'The wisdom of a man' — the tricolon (grizzly, puma, man) builds to the hilarious anticlimax of 'a man.' After the power of a grizzly and the reflexes of a puma, 'a man' is a comedically weak third element. Rex presents it as the crown of his offering
jokes.explanation: The tricolon structure ('strength of a grizzly / reflexes of a puma / wisdom of a man') is a genuinely well-constructed joke. The first two items set a pattern of powerful animals, so 'wisdom of a man' is a perfect anticlimax — it's both the weakest of the three and also slightly insulting to 'man' by comparison with grizzlies and pumas. Rex's total self-seriousness makes it funnier. The structure is near-perfect (9.0): setup, escalation, anticlimax punchline. Very quotable. Rex Kwon Do is one of the film's most beloved comedy bits.

jokes.text: Well, maybe you'd be interested in some home-woven handicrafts.
jokes.setup: Deb's glamour shot pitch has been rejected.
jokes.punchline: Without missing a beat, Deb pivots to home-woven handicrafts — revealing this is a multi-product sales operation and that Deb is pursuing multiple small-business income streams simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: The pivot reveals the full scope of Deb's entrepreneurial hustle and the slight desperation underneath it. The escalation from glamour shots to 'home-woven handicrafts' is funny precisely because these are unrelated product categories — she's just trying everything.

jokes.text: 'In here we have some boondoggle key chains. A must-have for this season's fashion.' / 'I already made, like, infinity of those at Scout camp.'
jokes.setup: Deb pivots from glamour shots to selling hand-woven boondoggle key chains as a fashion item
jokes.punchline: Napoleon has already made 'like, infinity of those at Scout camp' — infinite key chains, rendering Deb's product valueless to him. 'Infinity' as a quantity is a perfect Napoleon hyperbole
jokes.explanation: 'Like, infinity' is a great Napoleon-ism — the hedging 'like' modifying the absolute 'infinity' is exactly his register. The joke works because Napoleon deflects every sales pitch with an accidental perfect counter. He's not trying to be funny; he just genuinely made infinite key chains. Good economy.

jokes.text: 'Your mom goes to college.'
jokes.setup: Deb says 'I'm trying to earn money for college'
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's non sequitur retort: 'Your mom goes to college' — a playground-level comeback that makes no sense as a response to what Deb said, delivered with apparent sincerity
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the entire film. 'Your mom goes to college' is funny because it's the ur-example of a 'your mom' joke that makes absolutely no sense — going to college isn't an insult, and it has no logical connection to Deb's statement. Napoleon uses it as a devastating comeback to something that required no comeback. The randomness IS the joke, but it's not random in a cheap way — it's entirely consistent with Napoleon's social incompetence and his belief that he's winning this interaction. Economy is 10 (five words, one of the most memorable lines in the movie). Quotability is 10 — this became a cultural phrase.

jokes.text: 'Tina, you fat lard. Come get some dinner.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon goes out to feed an animal — which turns out to be a llama named Tina
jokes.punchline: Napoleon addresses the llama as 'Tina, you fat lard' — the contrast between a sweet, humanizing name ('Tina') and the brutal assessment ('fat lard') delivered with complete casualness is the joke. Also: they have a llama
jokes.explanation: One of the film's iconic moments. 'Tina, you fat lard' works on multiple levels: the reveal that Tina is a llama (visual gag), Napoleon's total unselfconsciousness about the insult, and the word 'lard' — not 'pig' or 'fatty' but the specific rendered animal fat product. The name 'Tina' for a llama is perfect. This is a character joke that could ONLY come from Napoleon and this household. Very high quotability — 'Tina, you fat lard' is probably the most quoted line from this film.

jokes.text: 'Tina, eat. Eat the food. / Eat the food!'
jokes.setup: Napoleon tells Tina to come eat; Tina (the llama) presumably refuses
jokes.punchline: Napoleon escalates from polite request ('Tina, eat') to increasingly desperate commands ('Eat the food! / Eat the food!') — he's trying to force a llama to comply through the power of repetition and rising frustration
jokes.explanation: The escalating demands are funny because Napoleon treats the llama like a stubborn child he has authority over — the gap between his assertiveness and the llama's indifference is the joke. 'Eat the food' (not 'your food' or 'the dinner') is a weirdly impersonal phrasing that adds to the absurdity. Good callback payoff to joke #31.

jokes.text: Napoleon on a horse being dragged into town: 'It'd be nice if you could pull me into town.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon is apparently being pulled behind a horse — a visually absurd image of a teenager passively dragged across the landscape
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's understatement: 'It'd be nice if you could pull me into town' — delivered as a mild suggestion rather than a desperate request, as if being dragged by a horse is a reasonable transportation option he's just gently proposing
jokes.explanation: Classic deadpan understatement — the visual gag (Napoleon dragged by horse) is the primary joke, and 'It'd be nice if you could pull me into town' is the perfect verbal complement: polite, reasonable-sounding, and completely incongruous with the situation. Napoleon's equanimity in physically absurd situations is a consistent character trait.

jokes.text: Rex Kwon Do infomercial continues: 'Bow to your sensei. Bow to your sensei!' — Rex barks at a reluctant volunteer
jokes.setup: Rex is demonstrating his self-defense system live; he calls up a volunteer
jokes.punchline: Rex's aggressive 'Bow to your sensei!' — repeated twice — reveals his desperate need for respect and submission. The doubling of the command because the person doesn't bow immediately is the cringe joke: Rex is a small man performing massive authority
jokes.explanation: Rex's need to repeat the bow command is a perfect character reveal — the man who promised the 'wisdom of a man' has to shout at someone twice to get a bow. The gap between Rex's self-image and his actual authority is the sustained comedy engine of his scenes. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Rex's self-defense demonstration: 'I'm just gonna break the wrist and walk away. Break the wrist, walk away.'
jokes.setup: Rex is demonstrating his signature Rex Kwon Do technique on a live volunteer
jokes.punchline: 'Break the wrist, walk away' — Rex repeats his technique as a memorable slogan, as though it's a profound martial arts philosophy. The casualness of 'walk away' after the violence of 'break the wrist' is funny. The repetition as if it's a mantra adds to it
jokes.explanation: One of the best Rex Kwon Do jokes. 'Break the wrist, walk away' is a great piece of comedy writing: it's violent, it's simple, it's rhythmic, and Rex repeats it as a teaching mantra as though it's Sun Tzu. The economy is exceptional — four words encode the whole character (Rex's violence, his self-satisfaction, his simple-minded philosophy). The technique also sounds like it would actually hurt, which makes the casual 'walk away' funnier. High quotability — this became a memorable film phrase.

jokes.text: Rex's first principle: 'No more flyin' solo. You need somebody watching your back at all times!' — Rex Kwon Do uses the buddy system
jokes.setup: Rex is listing the principles of Rex Kwon Do; the audience expects martial arts wisdom
jokes.punchline: The first principle of this self-defense system is... the buddy system. Rex presents this children's field-trip safety rule as cutting-edge tactical doctrine with complete gravitas
jokes.explanation: The buddy system as a Rex Kwon Do principle is a great deflation of the martial arts genre. Rex has built up his system as something formidable, and Principle #1 is something you learn on a kindergarten field trip. 'No more flyin' solo' repackages it in action-movie language that makes the reveal funnier. Good structure and originality.

jokes.text: Rex Kwon Do Principle 2: 'You're gonna learn to discipline your image. Do you think I got where I am today because I dress like Peter Pan here? Do you think anybody wants a roundhouse kick to the face while I'm wearin' these bad boys?'
jokes.setup: Rex's second principle is 'discipline your image'; he gestures to his own outfit as an example
jokes.punchline: Rex calls a presumably normal-looking person 'Peter Pan,' then asks if anyone wants a roundhouse kick while he's wearing his American flag pants — presenting his patriotic martial arts outfit as an intimidation multiplier. The flag pants are a visual gag that the dialogue confirms
jokes.explanation: 'Do you think anybody wants a roundhouse kick to the face while I'm wearin' these bad boys?' works because Rex is completely serious: the American flag pants are, in his mind, a legitimate combat advantage. The 'Peter Pan' insult for someone who is presumably dressed normally is a great character detail — Rex sees himself as elevated above ordinary fashion. The flag pants as a visual gag anchor the whole bit.

jokes.text: Rex Kwon Do Principle 3: 'Do you think anybody thinks I'm a failure because I go home to Starla at night? Forget about it!'
jokes.setup: Rex's third principle is 'self-respect'; he uses his personal life as evidence of his success
jokes.punchline: The evidence of Rex's success is 'going home to Starla' — his wife/girlfriend, whose name alone is funny. Rex frames this personal relationship as a public triumph others must acknowledge. The rhetorical 'Forget about it!' borrowed from tough-guy film vernacular applied to this mundane situation is the kicker
jokes.explanation: Rex's self-respect principle being anchored in 'going home to Starla' is funny because (a) Starla is a perfect name for Rex's wife, (b) Rex presents his domestic life as a public achievement, and (c) 'Forget about it' as his rhetorical flourish borrows Mafia-movie authority for this Idaho living situation. The question 'do you think anybody thinks I'm a failure' implies Rex is aware of the possibility — which makes his confidence funnier.

jokes.text: Do you think anybody thinks I'm a failure because I go home to Starla at night? Forget about it!
jokes.setup: Rex is making his pitch for self-respect as the third principle of Rex Kwon Do.
jokes.punchline: Rex's proof of his success in life is 'Starla' — the name implies a very specific type of woman who would partner with a Rex. The confidence with which he deploys this as a trump card, plus a second 'Forget about it!', suggests Rex uses Starla as his ultimate rebuttal to any criticism.
jokes.explanation: The name 'Starla' is doing a lot of work — it's a name that implies a certain social world and life trajectory that perfectly fits Rex. Rex's rhetorical question presupposes that going home to Starla is an objectively enviable outcome, which the audience may not share. The repeated 'Forget about it!' has escalated into Rex's verbal tic and battle cry.

jokes.text: 'Well, that place was a rip-off.' — Napoleon after leaving Rex Kwon Do
jokes.setup: Napoleon has just watched Rex Kwon Do's full pitch — a free trial lesson that included watching Rex bully a volunteer and listing principles like 'the buddy system'
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's verdict: 'That place was a rip-off' — despite the lesson being free. Napoleon's consumerism critique is applied to something he received for free, delivered with weary certainty
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Rex Kwon Do sequence. Napoleon calling a free trial lesson a 'rip-off' is funny because his consumer logic is broken — he got exactly what was advertised (a free trial) and found it worthless. It also characterizes Napoleon as someone who feels perpetually cheated by the world. Great economy.

jokes.text: 'Nothin' on here works smooth.' — Napoleon on a tractor or farm equipment at Lyle's
jokes.setup: Napoleon is apparently operating some farm equipment and finds it lacking
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's expert assessment — 'Nothin' on here works smooth' — delivered as the judgment of a connoisseur of smooth-working farm equipment
jokes.explanation: Minor joke. Napoleon's casual expertise about farm equipment functionality is mildly funny as another expression of his all-encompassing critical judgment of everything around him. Weaker than similar beats in the reel.

jokes.text: 'So me and you are pretty much friends by now, right?' / 'Yes.' / 'So, you got my back and everything?' / 'What?' / 'Never mind.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon and Pedro are eating lunch together; Napoleon seeks to formalize their friendship
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's negotiation of friendship terms — specifically asking Pedro to confirm he 'has his back' — is awkwardly transactional. When Pedro doesn't understand 'got my back,' Napoleon immediately retreats: 'Never mind' — suggesting the whole thing is too painful to explain
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny. Napoleon's attempt to verify friendship status is both socially awkward and oddly touching. 'So you got my back and everything?' as a formal friendship confirmation question is great character work. The immediate 'Never mind' when Pedro doesn't understand shows Napoleon's social fragility — he wants the alliance but can't survive the vulnerability of explaining it. The deadpan 'Yes' from Pedro to 'pretty much friends by now, right?' — as if checking a box — is also funny.

jokes.text: 'Who you gonna ask?' / 'That girl over there.' / 'She braided my hair one time—' / 'Summer Wheatly? How the heck are you gonna do that?'
jokes.setup: Pedro says he'll ask a girl to the dance after school; Napoleon asks who
jokes.punchline: Pedro's intended dance date is Summer Wheatly — apparently an aspirationally unattainable girl. Napoleon's reaction — 'How the heck are you gonna do that?' — is a mix of genuine curiosity and implied impossibility. Napoleon's credential for knowing Summer is that she 'braided his hair one time'
jokes.explanation: 'She braided my hair one time' as Napoleon's basis for knowing Summer is a funny detail — it implies a brief, one-sided interaction that Napoleon has catalogued as a meaningful social connection. 'How the heck are you gonna do that?' is classic Napoleon skepticism toward others despite his own total lack of social capital. Good character work.

jokes.text: 'Build her a cake or something.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon asks how Pedro is going to ask Summer Wheatly to the dance
jokes.punchline: Pedro's answer — 'Build her a cake or something' — is delivered as a reasonable, obvious strategy. The 'or something' hedge makes it funnier, as does the word 'build' rather than 'bake' — Pedro treats the cake as an engineering project
jokes.explanation: One of Pedro's best lines. 'Build her a cake' is funny because (a) 'build' not 'bake,' implying construction rather than cooking, (b) it's said as a matter-of-fact strategy without any apparent awareness of how odd this is, and (c) Pedro delivers it with absolute certainty. The 'or something' at the end is a perfect lazy hedge. This is excellent character integration — Pedro's earnest, slightly alien approach to romance is captured perfectly in three words. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Build her a cake or something.
jokes.setup: Napoleon has just asked Pedro how he's going to ask Summer to the dance.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's strategic advice: 'Build her a cake or something.' As if cake construction is the standard courtship move, and 'or something' acknowledges this might be too specific.
jokes.explanation: Five words of absurdist romantic advice. 'Build her a cake' (not 'make' or 'bake' — 'build') implies a certain structural ambition, and 'or something' as the hedge is perfect. Napoleon delivers this with the confidence of someone who has thought deeply about romance strategy. Very economy-efficient.

jokes.text: Napoleon's girlfriend from Oklahoma: 'Yeah, my old girlfriend from Oklahoma was gonna fly out here for the dance, but she couldn't 'cause she's doing some modeling right now.'
jokes.setup: Pedro and Napoleon are discussing the dance; Napoleon unexpectedly volunteers information about his own girlfriend situation
jokes.punchline: Napoleon has an 'old girlfriend from Oklahoma' who can't come because she's 'doing some modeling right now' — a tall tale so transparent it barely needs puncturing. The specific detail of Oklahoma and the specific excuse (modeling) confirm this is entirely invented
jokes.explanation: Napoleon's fabricated girlfriend is a classic character beat — the same impulse as the wolverine hunting story, now applied to romance. The 'modeling' excuse is perfect: sufficiently glamorous to impress, sufficiently vague to be unfalsifiable. The fact that Napoleon volunteers this information when no one asked is very Napoleon. Gets rewatch bonus because later in the film we discover Napoleon has actually mailed this 'girlfriend' a glamour shot.

jokes.text: Pedro shows Napoleon a photo of his girlfriend: 'See for yourself.' — Napoleon's reaction implied
jokes.setup: Napoleon asks 'Is she hot?' about Pedro's Oklahoma girlfriend
jokes.punchline: 'See for yourself' — Pedro produces a photo, implying the photo will speak for itself. The audience (and Napoleon) examine the photo. Napoleon's reaction determines the joke's payoff: either the photo confirms she's attractive or it's another Napoleon fabrication
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the glamour shot reveal. The 'See for yourself' is deadpan and confident — Pedro's willingness to show the photo suggests he's not ashamed. Gets rewatch bonus because on rewatch the glamour shot connection clicks. Moderate score as the transcript alone doesn't fully reveal the punchline visual.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, I took her to the mall to get some glamour shots for her birthday one year.' / 'I like her bangs.' / 'Me too.'
jokes.setup: Pedro's photo of his girlfriend is revealed to be a glamour shot; Napoleon and Pedro bond over their assessment of it
jokes.punchline: The mutual appreciation of the girlfriend's 'bangs' is funny because: (a) glamour shot girls always have specific 80s-adjacent bangs, (b) Napoleon and Pedro evaluating the photo together like art critics and landing on 'I like her bangs / Me too' is an oddly sincere, deadpan male-bonding moment, and (c) it's a callback to Deb's glamour shots door-to-door pitch earlier
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — 'I like her bangs / Me too' is four words that accomplish a lot. The deadpan sincerity of both characters complimenting the glamour shot's hairstyle is funny. The callback to Deb's glamour shots gives it structural payoff. This bonding moment over a tacky photo is both funny and character-revealing: Napoleon and Pedro have found common ground in aesthetic appreciation of a mall photo. The specificity of 'bangs' as the chosen compliment is perfect.

jokes.text: 'How long did it take you to grow that mustache?' / 'A couple of days.' / 'I wish I could grow one.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon and Pedro are bonding; Napoleon notices Pedro's mustache
jokes.punchline: Pedro grew his mustache in 'a couple of days' — delivered as a casual, biological fact — and Napoleon's response is sincere mustache-envy: 'I wish I could grow one.' The idea that Napoleon aspires to Pedro's sparse adolescent mustache is funny
jokes.explanation: Very economical joke. 'A couple of days' is deadpan — Pedro states this as if it's unremarkable, perhaps not even noticing it might be impressive. Napoleon's sincere admiration ('I wish I could grow one') establishes Pedro as aspirationally masculine relative to Napoleon. The understated male friendship dynamic is both funny and weirdly touching. High economy score for 15 words doing significant character work.

jokes.text: How long did it take you to grow that mustache? / A couple of days. / I wish I could grow one.
jokes.setup: Napoleon notices Pedro's mustache.
jokes.punchline: Pedro's claim that his mustache took 'a couple of days' (implying impressive and effortless facial hair growth), followed by Napoleon's sincere 'I wish I could grow one' — revealing mustache envy.
jokes.explanation: Perfect brief exchange. 'A couple of days' as the stated growth time for a full mustache, delivered by Pedro without pride or irony, followed by Napoleon's sincere 'I wish I could grow one' — the genuine longing in this is both funny and characterizes the Napoleon-Pedro dynamic beautifully. Napoleon covets Pedro's natural advantages (mustache, bike, ease with girls). Very quotable.

jokes.text: 'Are you gonna eat your Tots?' / 'No.' / 'Can I have 'em?'
jokes.setup: Napoleon and Pedro are eating lunch in the cafeteria
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's preoccupation with Pedro's Tater Tots — asked with the same gravity as his friendship and dance questions — implies that for Napoleon, food access is on the same tier as social bonding
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most iconic small moments. The Tater Tot exchange is funny because of perfect deadpan economy and because Napoleon transitions from friendship negotiation to food acquisition without any tonal shift — both are equally urgent to him. 'Can I have 'em?' is Napoleon at his most purely Napoleon. Gets rewatch bonus because later in the film the Tots pay off in a physical comedy bit. Near-maximum economy score.

jokes.text: 'You see that girl over there? She came over to my house the other day. Why? I don't know, but she left all this crap on my porch.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon points out a girl (Deb) across the cafeteria to Pedro
jokes.punchline: Napoleon describes Deb's door-to-door sales visit as her leaving 'all this crap on my porch' — characterizing her glamour shots and boondoggle key chains as garbage. He also genuinely doesn't know why she came over, which is funny given that she was running a small business
jokes.explanation: Callback to the Deb sequence. Napoleon's bafflement about why she came ('I don't know') despite having had a full conversation with her is funny — he was present for her entire sales pitch and apparently retained none of it except that she left 'crap.' The word 'crap' for key chains and glamour shots is consistent Napoleon dismissiveness. Good rewatch connection.

jokes.text: You see that girl over there? She came over to my house the other day. Why? I don't know, but she left all this crap on my porch.
jokes.setup: Napoleon points out Deb to Pedro.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's characterization of Deb's sales visit as her inexplicably leaving 'all this crap on my porch' — he has absolutely no insight into why she came and no apparent interest in finding out.
jokes.explanation: Callback to Deb's sales visit. Napoleon's interpretation of Deb's entrepreneurial visit as a mysterious crap-depositing event shows how completely he misread it. His complete lack of curiosity ('I don't know') about why a girl came to his house is both funny and consistent characterization.

jokes.text: 'She's pretty good-looking.' / 'Do you dare me to go talk to her?' / 'Sure.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon points Deb out as a girl who came to his house; Pedro notes she's good-looking
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's approach to talking to girls requires a dare — he asks Pedro to dare him as the social mechanism for action. Pedro's flat 'Sure' as consent to the dare is perfect. The 'dare' framing exposes Napoleon's total lack of natural social initiative
jokes.explanation: Napoleon needing to structure talking to a girl as a dare is a perfect character beat — the dare provides external permission he can't generate internally. Pedro's total lack of enthusiasm in 'Sure' is a good deadpan reaction. The whole thing anticipates the deeply awkward interaction that follows. High character integration: Napoleon's social mechanics are completely exposed here.

jokes.text: 'I see you're drinking one-percent. Is that 'cause you think you're fat? 'Cause you're not. You could be drinking whole if you wanted to.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon has dared himself to go talk to Deb; he walks up to her in the cafeteria
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's opening line to the girl he wants to impress is to comment on her milk choice as a potential indicator of body dysmorphia — 'Is that 'cause you think you're fat?' — and then immediately reassure her she could drink whole milk. This is objectively the worst possible opening gambit, delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the reel by a significant margin. Napoleon's milk observation is a perfect encapsulation of everything the film is about: Napoleon thinks he is making a smooth, complimentary approach. His logic is internally consistent (one-percent implies calorie-consciousness implies self-esteem issues, so he will compliment her by granting milk permission). The result is an insult that he has packaged as a compliment, delivered with total confidence. 'You could be drinking whole if you wanted to' as a benevolent milk-freedom offer is extraordinary. The structure is flawless — set up (milk observation), question (are you fat?), reassurance (you're not), punchline (whole milk offer). Character integration is 10 — no other character in cinema would do this. High originality because this specific joke construction has never existed before. It is a cultural touchstone from the film.

jokes.text: 'Well, I have all your equipment in my locker. You should probably come get it 'cause I can't fit my nunchakus in there anymore.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon is continuing his milk conversation with Deb, trying to extend the interaction
jokes.punchline: Napoleon pivots to telling Deb he has her glamour shots equipment and can't fit his nunchakus in his locker — the mention of nunchakus as a locker staple, stated casually, is the joke. Napoleon carries nunchakus to school
jokes.explanation: Napoleon keeps nunchakus in his school locker. This is revealed as a matter of practical constraint — he can't fit them anymore because of Deb's equipment. The casual nunchaku mention is excellent character-world-building: of course Napoleon has nunchakus at school. It also retroactively recontextualizes Napoleon's interest in Rex Kwon Do and bow staffs as part of a consistent weapons hobby. Very high character integration — this is specific to Napoleon and his world.

jokes.text: Well, I have all your equipment in my locker. You should probably come get it 'cause I can't fit my nunchakus in there anymore.
jokes.setup: Napoleon is continuing his conversation with Deb after the milk line.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's follow-up: he is in possession of her glamour shot equipment, which he has stored with his nunchakus — the coexistence of her equipment and his nunchakus in a school locker being inherently funny, and the nunchakus being his actual problem rather than any interest in returning her things.
jokes.explanation: The nunchakus in the locker is a great reveal — Napoleon has nunchakus at school, which he apparently stores without issue, and the reason he's mentioning Deb's equipment is because his nunchakus don't fit anymore. The practical concern (locker space) rather than any social grace (returning her things) is very Napoleon. This is a callback that also adds new information.

jokes.text: 'Hey, can I have one of your key chains?' — Napoleon to Deb as she leaves
jokes.setup: Napoleon told Deb earlier (joke #29) that he'd already made 'like, infinity' of boondoggle key chains at Scout camp and implicitly rejected her sales pitch
jokes.punchline: Napoleon now asks for one of Deb's key chains — he dismissed them as beneath him at his house but now requests one, possibly as a social move with Deb, possibly just because he wants one. The irony of asking after rejecting is the callback payoff
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Deb sequence across the whole reel. Napoleon rejected the key chains at his house, then called her stuff 'crap,' and now asks for a key chain — possibly as a clumsy flirtation move, possibly just because he forgot. The callback structure gives this 7-word scene-closing line more weight than it would have in isolation. Great economy and rewatch value as a structural payoff to the Deb thread.

jokes.text: Napoleon, give me some of your Tots. — No, go find your own. — I'm freakin' starved. I didn't get to eat anything today.
jokes.setup: A classmate asks Napoleon to share his cafeteria tater tots, a mundane request.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon refuses with dead seriousness and territorial ferocity over cafeteria tots, treating them like precious treasure.
jokes.explanation: The tater tots exchange is the film's most iconic running element. Napoleon's disproportionate protectiveness of cafeteria food is perfect character comedy — the deadpan refusal 'No, go find your own' treats tots as a matter of existential importance. High quotability and character integration; it defines Napoleon's self-absorbed obliviousness.

jokes.text: Napoleon pockets his tots, they get sat on/crushed, he pulls them out smashed — 'Gross. Freakin' idiot!'
jokes.setup: Napoleon refuses to share his tots and presumably shoves them in his pocket to protect them.
jokes.punchline: The tots are destroyed (sat upon or crushed), and Napoleon blames the other kid — the consequence of his own absurd hoarding.
jokes.explanation: The perfect escalation of the tots bit. Napoleon's choice to protect his tots by pocketing them backfires immediately, and his response is to blame someone else entirely — 'Freakin' idiot!' The structure is excellent: setup (refusal), complication (pocketing), punchline (destruction + misdirected rage). One of the reel's strongest physical comedy moments.

jokes.text: Tina, come get some ham.
jokes.setup: Napoleon arrives home after the school confrontation, still in a foul mood.
jokes.punchline: He immediately calls out to his llama, Tina, with the same flat, matter-of-fact tone he uses for everything — feeding a llama ham is treated as completely normal.
jokes.explanation: Five words. Perfect economy. The joke is entirely in the delivery and the absurdity of a pet llama being called Tina and fed ham as if it were the most ordinary thing. High quotability — this became one of the film's most memeable lines. The humor is in what is NOT explained or reacted to.

jokes.text: Your grandma took a little spill at the sand dunes today, broke her coccyx.
jokes.setup: Napoleon asks what Uncle Rico is doing at the house; a serious family emergency is implied.
jokes.punchline: The injury is a 'coccyx' fracture — an inherently funny word used with absolute straight-faced seriousness — and the cause is grandma being at sand dunes, which is unexpected.
jokes.explanation: Two-layered joke: the word 'coccyx' is funny on its own, and the revelation that grandma was at sand dunes at all is a secondary absurdist payoff. Competent but not exceptional — the coccyx joke is a well-worn comedy trope.

jokes.text: Looks like there's a lot you don't know about her.
jokes.setup: Napoleon expresses surprise that his grandmother was at sand dunes.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Rico delivers a melodramatically weighted line — 'Looks like there's a lot you don't know about her' — as if revealing a profound truth about a grandmother going to sand dunes.
jokes.explanation: Uncle Rico's self-important delivery of a banal observation is classic character comedy for him. The gap between the gravity of his tone and the triviality of the content (grandma having a social life) is the joke. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Well, Kip is, like, 32 years old.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico suggests he needs to stay to look after the boys, treating them as children.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon protests by citing Kip's age — 32 — as evidence they don't need a babysitter, while Kip immediately undermines this by saying 'I don't mind if you stay.'
jokes.explanation: The two-part joke works beautifully: Napoleon's deadpan citation of Kip's age implies Kip is capable and independent, then Kip immediately reveals his pathetic dependency by welcoming the babysitter. The structure is excellent — Napoleon sets up Kip's demolition of his own case.

jokes.text: She was on a date... with her boyfriend.
jokes.setup: Napoleon asks what grandma was doing at the sand dunes, expecting a mundane answer.
jokes.punchline: She was on a romantic date — grandma has a boyfriend — delivered with Uncle Rico's characteristic dramatic pause as if dropping a bombshell.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that grandma has an active romantic life is a mild absurdist payoff to a running question. The pause before 'with her boyfriend' is well-timed. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Man, I wish I could go back in time. I'd take state. — This is pretty much the worst video ever made. — Napoleon, like anyone can even know that.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico shows a home video of himself playing football in his glory days and asks what they think.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon brutally dismisses it as 'pretty much the worst video ever made' — but Kip defends Uncle Rico with the nonsensical retort 'like anyone can even know that,' which is both a defense and an accidental absurdism.
jokes.explanation: Triple-layered: Uncle Rico's delusional nostalgia ('I'd take state'), Napoleon's savagely accurate critique, and Kip's baffling non-defense that inadvertently sides with Uncle Rico through pseudo-philosophical logic. 'Like anyone can even know that' is highly quotable and perfectly characterizes Kip's dim earnestness.

jokes.text: You guys are retarded.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico kicks Napoleon out after his 'worst video' insult; Napoleon is ejected.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's exit line — delivered with complete conviction as the parting shot of a person who absolutely believes he is the most rational person in the room.
jokes.explanation: Napoleon's reflexive insult-and-exit is good character comedy but relatively thin. The word choice is blunt and the delivery carries it more than any structural cleverness.

jokes.text: She's jealous. Says I'm livin' too much in '82. Well, I dumped her.
jokes.setup: Kip asks Uncle Rico why he and Tammy aren't together anymore.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Rico first blames the girlfriend ('she's jealous'), then inadvertently confirms her critique by citing '82, then immediately contradicts his victim stance by claiming HE dumped HER.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. In three short sentences, Uncle Rico simultaneously validates his ex-girlfriend's exact complaint while denying it, then saves face by claiming he was the dumper. The self-contradiction happens so fast and with such conviction that it perfectly encapsulates his delusional, ego-protecting worldview. The structure is tight and the character specificity is high — only Uncle Rico delivers this particular flavor of oblivious machismo.

jokes.text: I mean, we chat online for, like, two hours every day, so I guess you could say things are gettin' pretty serious.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico asks about Kip's girlfriend; Kip describes their 'serious' relationship.
jokes.punchline: The evidence of seriousness is two hours of daily online chatting — Kip's earnest sincerity about this metric of romantic commitment is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures the early-internet-era pathetic romance with deadpan sincerity. 'So I guess you could say things are gettin' pretty serious' works because Kip is not being ironic at all — the two-hour chat sessions ARE his threshold for seriousness. Character-specific and of-its-era in a way that deepens on rewatch.

jokes.text: She's got sandy blonde hair... pretty good-looking face, but... I'm just gettin' really T.O.'d because she hasn't even sent me a full body shot yet.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico asks what the online girlfriend looks like; Kip begins describing her.
jokes.punchline: After diplomatically hedging on her face ('pretty good-looking... but'), Kip reveals his real frustration: no full body shot — a cringe-inducing window into his shallow, deluded priorities for a relationship that may not even be real.
jokes.explanation: The 'but' after 'pretty good-looking face' primes the audience for a complaint about personality or distance; instead the complaint is the absence of a full body photo, revealing both Kip's superficiality and the likely fictional nature of this online relationship. Well-structured misdirection with strong character integration.

jokes.text: Uncle Rico throws a football and it's later revealed he's been practicing his throw to impress Kip with his claim of being able to throw a pigskin a quarter mile.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico says he's got a 'little project' for making money; he takes Kip outside.
jokes.punchline: The 'project' reveal is Uncle Rico demonstrating his football throw in a field — his entrepreneurial scheme is entirely secondary to his need to prove his athletic past.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the larger Uncle Rico delusion sequence; works as character establishment but the visual comedy is inferred rather than punchline-driven in the dialogue itself.

jokes.text: Back in '82, I used to be able to throw a pigskin a quarter mile. — Are you serious? — I'm dead serious.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is about to demonstrate his football skills.
jokes.punchline: He prefaces it with the physically impossible boast — a quarter mile is 440 yards, far beyond any human capacity — delivered with absolute, earnest conviction. 'I'm dead serious' is the perfect straight-faced escalation.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes. The claim is absurd on its face — a quarter-mile throw is superhuman — but Uncle Rico states it with zero irony and doubles down with 'I'm dead serious.' This encapsulates his entire character: the delusion is not comedic exaggeration to him, it is his sincere self-image. The economy is superb, the character integration is near-perfect, and it became one of the film's most quoted lines. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its quotability and character specificity.

jokes.text: How much you want to make a bet I can throw a football over them mountains?
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico has just thrown a football that clearly didn't go a quarter mile.
jokes.punchline: Undeterred by reality, he escalates to betting he can throw it OVER MOUNTAINS — the delusion spiraling upward even as the evidence contradicts it.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'quarter mile' to 'over them mountains' is a perfect comedic build — each claim larger than the last, each delivered with equal sincerity. The visual of mountains in the background makes this a visual gag as well. Highly quotable and captures the film's signature deadpan absurdism.

jokes.text: You know, soakin' it up in a hot tub with my soul mate.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico's fantasy escalates through state champion, pro career, millions, mansion.
jokes.punchline: The crowning detail of the fantasy is soaking in a hot tub with his 'soul mate' — the specific, intimate domesticity of the image after the grand athletic claims is an unexpected and funny landing point.
jokes.explanation: The landing of the fantasy on 'hot tub with my soul mate' is a tonal shift from athletic glory to domestic comfort that undercuts the grandiosity in a quietly funny way. Uncle Rico's sincerity makes it poignant-funny rather than purely absurd.

jokes.text: Easy. I've already looked into it for myself.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico asks if Kip has come across time travel on cyberspace.
jokes.punchline: Kip responds with 'Easy' — as if the question is a gimme — and reveals he has 'already looked into it for myself,' treating time travel research as a normal thing one does.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes. 'Easy' is doing enormous work — it signals Kip's misplaced confidence — and 'I've already looked into it for myself' implies he, too, has personal reasons for wanting time travel (his sad online romance? his arrested development?). The economy is exceptional: two sentences that simultaneously characterize Kip as deluded and incompetent while being completely earnest. The 'for myself' detail is the hidden gem.

jokes.text: What are you drawing? — A liger. — What's a liger? — It's pretty much my favorite animal. It's like a lion and a tiger mixed. Bred for its skills in magic.
jokes.setup: Deb notices Napoleon drawing something in class and asks what it is.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon describes the liger with complete taxonomic authority, culminating in 'Bred for its skills in magic' — an entirely invented attribute stated as biological fact.
jokes.explanation: The liger speech is the reel's single best joke and among the film's most iconic moments. The structure is perfect: Napoleon establishes factual-sounding taxonomy ('lion and a tiger mixed'), then pivots to 'Bred for its skills in magic' — a phrase with zero logical meaning stated with complete zoological confidence. The word 'bred' suggests scientific breeding programs, while 'skills in magic' is pure fantasy. Only Napoleon could deliver this with no awareness of its absurdity. Became a cultural touchstone. Easily the reel's standout joke.

jokes.text: Napoleon notes Pedro hasn't been in school; we learn he missed the bus but his uncle is picking him up — reaction beat of Napoleon's flat non-reaction to this information.
jokes.setup: Napoleon and Deb discuss that Pedro hasn't been seen at school.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's complete lack of emotional investment or curiosity — asking if Pedro needs a ride and then accepting 'No' with zero follow-up — is a deadpan reaction beat that plays against normal social concern.
jokes.explanation: Minor atmospheric beat. Napoleon's flat social affect is consistent character work but this instance doesn't have a specific comedic payoff — it's characterization more than joke.

jokes.text: Just a little bit east of the cemetery is a good little area right here. We should do it there. Don't go down here, 'cause they don't have any money.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is mapping out a door-to-door sales route with Kip.
jokes.punchline: He casually dismisses an entire neighborhood based on assumed poverty — 'they don't have any money' — with the same matter-of-fact confidence he applies to all his schemes.
jokes.explanation: Minor joke — Uncle Rico's casual classism/pragmatism is in character but not especially sharp. Works as world-building for the sales scheme subplot.

jokes.text: Yeah. Grandma's still payin' per minute. She gets kind of pissed at me sometimes 'cause I'm on there so long. — I'll bet she does. I'd be throwin' you out the window.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico asks if the chat room costs money; Kip confirms grandma pays per-minute dial-up fees.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Rico's reaction — 'I'd be throwin' you out the window' — is a sudden burst of violence as a logical response, delivered with complete casualness.
jokes.explanation: Uncle Rico's threat of defenestration as a measured parenting response is good character comedy — his gruff machismo expressed through hyperbolic violence stated with matter-of-fact calm. The beat between 'I'll bet she does' (relatable frustration) and the escalation to window-throwing works well.

jokes.text: Who's this? — Napoleon Dynamite. — Who? — Napoleon Dynamite.
jokes.setup: Napoleon calls Pedro's house; a family member answers.
jokes.punchline: The name 'Napoleon Dynamite' prompts genuine confusion and a repeated 'Who?' — the name is so unusual that even stated twice it doesn't register as a real person's name.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the name itself functioning as a punchline — 'Napoleon Dynamite' is so absurd a name that the other person's disbelief ('Who?') is completely reasonable. Napoleon's repeated straight-faced confirmation deepens the deadpan. The film's title is the joke.

jokes.text: Napoleon calls Pedro's house; a family member answers. Napoleon introduces himself: 'Napoleon Dynamite.' The relative: 'Your name is Napoleon?'
jokes.setup: Napoleon calls to speak to Pedro and states his name
jokes.punchline: Pedro's cousin's incredulous echo — 'Your name is Napoleon?' — voices the audience's evergreen bewilderment at the name
jokes.explanation: A reliable but slight gag — the name is funny, someone reacts to it. The deadpan double-take is a reliable comedy tool and the film uses it correctly here, but it's not particularly inventive. Works as a character texture joke.

jokes.text: I'm one of Pedro's best friends.
jokes.setup: Napoleon tries to establish his identity and credibility on the phone.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon has known Pedro for approximately two days at this point — his self-designation as 'one of Pedro's best friends' reflects his complete lack of social awareness about how friendships develop.
jokes.explanation: Minor but authentic character joke — Napoleon's social obliviousness extends to claiming best-friend status with someone he barely knows. Works in context as character reinforcement.

jokes.text: Please. Please. Be good to me. Please, keep going. Dead on. Dead on. — Yes!
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is filming himself throwing a football for his video submission / sales material.
jokes.punchline: His whispered, intimate encouragement to himself ('Please. Be good to me. Dead on.') treats the act of throwing a football alone in a field as a profound, nearly religious event.
jokes.explanation: Uncle Rico filming himself and whispering desperate encouragement to his own throw is a quietly great character moment. The prayer-like intensity ('Please. Be good to me') applied to solo football practice reveals the depths of his delusion and longing. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Rico presents Kip's concern: 'We need some way to make us look official, like we got all the answers.' Kip: 'How about some gold bracelets?'
jokes.setup: Rico identifies the need for professional legitimacy in their door-to-door scheme
jokes.punchline: Kip's sincere suggestion is gold bracelets — not business cards, uniforms, or ID — gold bracelets
jokes.explanation: The gap between 'make us look official' and 'gold bracelets' is perfect absurdist logic — Kip has his own aesthetic sensibility that is entirely his own. It's a compact, well-structured character joke with strong economy.

jokes.text: Now, make a fist and slowly ease it up underneath your chin. — This is looking really good. — You can say that again.
jokes.setup: Deb is photographing Uncle Rico for the fake ID/name-tag project; she gives him modeling direction.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Rico takes the absurd 'fist under chin' pose seriously and responds to 'this is looking really good' with earnest 'you can say that again' — a vain man delighted by any compliment about his appearance.
jokes.explanation: Uncle Rico's vanity is well-served by the photo session. His 'you can say that again' — validating a hollow compliment — is consistent character work. The visual of grown men doing Sears Portrait Studio poses in a teenager's photography setup is inherently funny.

jokes.text: Now, just imagine you're weightless. You're in the middle of the ocean, surrounded by tiny little sea horses.
jokes.setup: Deb is directing Uncle Rico for his ID photo and tells him to 'hold still right there.'
jokes.punchline: Instead of a normal photographer's direction ('smile,' 'say cheese'), Deb delivers a surrealist meditation on weightlessness and seahorses — apparently her standard technique, delivered with complete normalcy.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's standout jokes. The specificity of the seahorse visualization is what elevates this from generic absurdism to genuine comic craft — it's not just 'imagine somewhere peaceful,' it's 'tiny little sea horses.' Deb's earnest belief that this is good photography direction, combined with Uncle Rico apparently believing it, makes this a perfect deadpan absurdist moment. Highly quotable and character-specific.

jokes.text: That was the one. I think that's gonna come out really nice. — Uh, you did it? — Wow. Wow, that felt really relaxed.
jokes.setup: Deb tells Uncle Rico she got the shot after the seahorse meditation.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Rico's response is 'Wow. That felt really relaxed' — confirming the seahorse technique worked on him, and that his standard state is apparently not relaxed. The 'Wow. Wow.' double-take is a perfectly timed reaction beat.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the seahorse bit. Uncle Rico's genuine surprise at feeling relaxed — 'Wow. Wow, that felt really relaxed' — plays as both a callback reward and a character note. The implication that this tightly wound man has rarely felt relaxed is a quietly funny layer.

jokes.text: Is there some kind of vest that I can wear?
jokes.setup: Kip is about to have his photo taken for the fake sales ID.
jokes.punchline: Kip's only concern is whether a vest is available — a 32-year-old man in rural Idaho whose primary contribution to a business meeting is a request for a vest.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that say everything about Kip's character. His contribution to business preparation is aesthetics (a vest), and his deadpan delivery of this request as if it's a reasonable professional concern is classic Kip. Becomes funnier on rewatch knowing his eventual fashion sensibility.

jokes.text: Well, nobody's gonna go out with me.
jokes.setup: Pedro asks if Napoleon has asked anyone to the dance; Napoleon admits he hasn't.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's flat self-assessment — 'nobody's gonna go out with me' — delivered without self-pity or irony, just factual resignation, is both funny and unexpectedly affecting.
jokes.explanation: Minor character moment — Napoleon's total unsentimental acceptance of his social status is in character, but this is more pathos than comedy. The deadpan delivery saves it from being merely sad.

jokes.text: You know, like... nunchaku skills, bow hunting skills, computer hacking skills. Girls only want boyfriends who have great skills.
jokes.setup: Napoleon explains to Pedro that he has no 'good skills' and therefore can't get a date.
jokes.punchline: His list of 'skills' — nunchaku, bow hunting, computer hacking — reveals a worldview of desirable masculine attributes that is entirely 1980s action movie logic, stated as contemporary dating wisdom.
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most quotable and iconic speeches. The specificity of 'nunchaku skills, bow hunting skills, computer hacking skills' creates a perfect comedic list — each item escalates the absurdity while maintaining Napoleon's internal logic (all are, to him, real masculine skill sets). The declarative 'Girls only want boyfriends who have great skills' is delivered as universal truth. Only Napoleon could arrive at this theory of romance, making the character integration near-perfect. Comparable to the craft 8.0 anchor and exceeds it in character specificity and quotability.

jokes.text: I bet you folks don't have one of these. [produces a miniature sailboat as a gift with a 24-piece bowl set]
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is mid-sales pitch for a 24-piece nylon polymer bowl set.
jokes.punchline: The 'gift' included with a 24-piece bowl set is a tiny decorative sailboat — a comically incongruous and worthless bonus item presented with enormous showman confidence.
jokes.explanation: The mini sailboat reveal is a good visual gag — the customer's desire ('I want that') for a worthless tchotchke is an absurd detail, and Uncle Rico's showmanship around it lampoons infomercial culture. The customer wanting the sailboat more than the actual product is a sharp comedic observation.

jokes.text: You see, this ain't your run-of-the-mill 'crapper-ware.' These are some serious 'NuPont' fiber-woven bowls.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is pitching the bowl set to potential customers.
jokes.punchline: He invents the term 'crapper-ware' as a category of inferior bowls, then positions 'NuPont' fiber-woven bowls as premium — the fake brand name rhyming with DuPont while implying new and innovative.
jokes.explanation: 'Crapper-ware' is a genuinely funny coinage — it sounds exactly like a real dismissive product category — and 'NuPont' is a subtle wordplay on DuPont that positions the product as aspirationally legitimate while being transparent nonsense. Uncle Rico's sales patter is pitch-perfect con-man comedy.

jokes.text: Lance, you look like a strong young pup. Why don't you see if you can give that a nice tear.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is demonstrating the durability of the NuPont bowls to potential customers.
jokes.punchline: He singles out 'Lance' — a presumably average-looking man — with the flattering 'strong young pup' and challenges him to tear the bowl, setting up an audience participation moment.
jokes.explanation: Classic infomercial flattery played for character comedy. 'Strong young pup' as an attempt at manly camaraderie is funny coming from Uncle Rico, whose own athletic confidence is pathetically misplaced.

jokes.text: Don't hurt yourself now. — I can't do it. — Can't do it.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico challenges Lance to tear the bowl; Lance actually can't do it.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Rico's preemptive 'Don't hurt yourself now' — meant as a funny caveat to a prop demonstration — accidentally becomes sincere advice, and his echoed 'Can't do it' at the end is delivered with salesman satisfaction.
jokes.explanation: A functional sales-pitch comedy beat. The bowl actually can't be torn, which is simultaneously a successful product demonstration and a commentary on Uncle Rico's hucksterism — these are perhaps genuine NuPont bowls. Mildly funny but not exceptional.

jokes.text: So, uh, how does the 'dealio' sound to you?
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico concludes his NuPont bowl sales pitch.
jokes.punchline: 'Dealio' — a slang diminutive for 'deal' — emerging from a man performing a formal business pitch. The word is a small but perfectly chosen bit of Uncle Rico's aspirational-yet-rural vernacular.
jokes.explanation: Minor word-choice joke. 'Dealio' is a funny collision of Uncle Rico's sales-pitch formality and his genuine Idaho vernacular. Small but authentic.

jokes.text: Poor kid. I've been takin' care of him while his grandma's in the hospital. He still wets the bed and everything.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is at a customer's door and Napoleon has just left after delivering the drawing to Trisha's house.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Rico volunteers that Napoleon still wets the bed — an intimate, embarrassing detail he has no business sharing with a stranger — as casual small talk to maintain the sales visit.
jokes.explanation: Uncle Rico weaponizing Napoleon's bedwetting as casual sales-call small talk is a sharp joke — it's simultaneously an overshare, a betrayal of confidence, and a transparent attempt to seem relatable to the customer. 'He still wets the bed and everything' with 'and everything' implying a whole catalog of shameful conditions is excellent. The 'tender little guy' follow-up adds a mock-compassionate layer.

jokes.text: Yeah, he's a tender little guy. He still gets beat up and whatnot.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico has just disclosed Napoleon's bedwetting to a stranger.
jokes.punchline: He adds that Napoleon 'still gets beat up and whatnot' — escalating the catalog of Napoleon's humiliations, with 'and whatnot' suggesting there's even more he's not listing.
jokes.explanation: The 'and whatnot' is doing real work here — it implies a list of Napoleon's shortcomings too long to enumerate, and it's delivered with the same casual compassion as a neighborhood gossip. Good escalation of the previous joke.

jokes.text: Ow! What the crap was Uncle Rico doin' at my girlfriend's house?
jokes.setup: Napoleon has apparently been lurking and watching Uncle Rico's sales visit at Trisha's house.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's indignation — 'my girlfriend's house' for a girl he's asked to a school dance — combined with the 'ow' suggesting he either reacted physically or was sneaking and hurt himself reveals both his territorial feelings and his social cluelessness.
