jokes.explanation: Napoleon designating Trisha as 'my girlfriend' when he has only asked her (and not yet received a yes) is consistent character work. The 'ow' is a minor physical comedy beat. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Napoleon, let go of me! I think you're bruisin' my neck meat!
jokes.setup: Napoleon confronts Kip about accompanying Uncle Rico on sales visits to Napoleon's 'girlfriend's' house.
jokes.punchline: Kip's complaint is not about the confrontation itself but the specific zone of injury — 'neck meat' — an anatomically precise yet somehow absurd term delivered with aggrieved dignity by a man being grabbed by his teenage brother.
jokes.explanation: 'Neck meat' is the joke — it's a real anatomical area but the word 'meat' applied to one's own body with the precise concern for it being 'bruised' is unexpectedly funny. Kip's indignation over this specific body part while being physically handled by his little brother is perfect Kip.

jokes.text: Geez, I think you ripped my mole off. — I did? — Yeah, is it bleeding? — A little bit.
jokes.setup: Napoleon releases Kip from his grip; the confrontation has apparently been physical.
jokes.punchline: Kip's mole has been ripped off — a grotesque escalation from 'bruisin' my neck meat' — and Napoleon's 'I did?' followed by the clinical check for bleeding treats a potentially serious injury with total flat affect.
jokes.explanation: The ripped-off mole escalates the physical comedy of the altercation in an unexpected direction. Napoleon's curiosity ('I did?') rather than concern, and the matter-of-fact 'A little bit' confirming bleeding, treats a grotesque injury with the same flat register as everything else in the film. Good escalation.

jokes.text: While you're playin' patty-cake with your friend Pedro, your Uncle Rico is makin' 120 bucks. — I could make that much money in five seconds. — Geez. Yeah, right, Napoleon. I made, like, 75 bucks today.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico taunts Napoleon about the money he's making while Napoleon hangs out with Pedro.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's claim ('five seconds') is immediately deflated by Kip, who points out Uncle Rico made $75 — not $120 as claimed — inadvertently contradicting his boss while still mocking Napoleon.
jokes.explanation: The three-way dynamic works well: Uncle Rico exaggerates his earnings, Napoleon overestimates his own potential, and Kip fact-corrects both while trying to side with Uncle Rico. The deflation of $120 to $75 is a subtle joke about Uncle Rico's unreliability even as a braggart.

jokes.text: Napoleon, it looks like you don't have a job. So why don't you get out there and feed Tina. — Why don't you go eat a 'decroded' piece of rap.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico dismisses Napoleon as unemployed and assigns him the chore of feeding the llama.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's comeback — 'go eat a decroded piece of rap' — is a malapropism-laden insult that makes no literal sense but is delivered with complete conviction. 'Decroded' may be a mash-up of 'decrepit' and 'corroded.'
jokes.explanation: Napoleon's invented insult vocabulary is peak character comedy. 'Decroded' is a word that doesn't exist but sounds exactly like it should be an insult, and 'piece of rap' instead of 'piece of crap' adds a second malapropism layer. The entire insult is semantically empty but emotionally fully loaded. High quotability and character integration — only Napoleon coins his own insults from corrupted vocabulary.

jokes.text: There's a lot more where this came from... if you go to the dance with me. Yours truly, Napoleon Dynamite.
jokes.setup: Napoleon has drawn a portrait of Trisha and left it as a note asking her to the dance.
jokes.punchline: The formal letter-signing 'Yours truly, Napoleon Dynamite' — as if the note were a business communication — combined with the portrait being his best romantic offering, captures Napoleon's complete social obliviousness.
jokes.explanation: 'Yours truly, Napoleon Dynamite' as a romantic overture sign-off is perfectly in character — formal, oblivious, and oddly touching. The 'there's a lot more where this came from' implying more portraits is both a threat and a promise.

jokes.text: Do the chickens have large talons? — Do they have what? — Large talons. — I don't understand a word you just said.
jokes.setup: Napoleon is getting instructions for a farm job moving chickens; the farmer describes the chickens.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's question about whether the chickens have 'large talons' is a completely irrelevant and oddly specific zoological inquiry mid-job-briefing, and the farmer's flat 'I don't understand a word you just said' is the perfect straight-man response.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes. Napoleon's concern about chicken talon size is simultaneously characteristic (his random animal obsessions) and completely inappropriate to the work context. The farmer's 'I don't understand a word you just said' is the ideal deadpan response — not confusion about the word 'talon' per se, but bewilderment at the entire question. The specificity of 'large talons' (rather than just 'do chickens have talons?') is what makes it exceptional. Comparable to the craft 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Napoleon: 'Do the chickens have large talons?' Farmer: 'Do they have what?' Napoleon: 'Large talons.' Farmer: 'I don't understand a word you just said.'
jokes.setup: The farmer has just explained the chicken job; Napoleon's response is a question about talons
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's concern is not about pay, hours, or difficulty — it's specifically whether the chickens have large talons; the farmer cannot process this question
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. Napoleon's first and only question about his new job is whether the chickens have large talons — a concern that makes internal sense for Napoleon (he draws warriors and creatures, he respects animals with 'skills') but is completely baffling to any normal employer. The farmer's 'I don't understand a word you just said' is the perfect straight-man response. Perfect economy, perfectly character-integrated, structurally clean, massively quotable. Near the top of the anchor scale.

jokes.text: 'Ew!' — Napoleon's reaction, inferred as he sees/handles something disgusting on the farm
jokes.setup: Napoleon is now working on the farm moving hens
jokes.punchline: The single-syllable expression of disgust — probably encountering chicken waste or an unpleasant farm reality — is a character-perfect response
jokes.explanation: A visual/reaction beat that plays better on screen. Napoleon's disgust is in character but without seeing the specific visual, the transcript-only delivery is a simple reaction. Modest score reflects that this is a visual gag dependent on what's on screen.

jokes.text: Over there, in that pigpen, I found a couple of Shoshoni arrowheads.
jokes.setup: Napoleon has completed his day of chicken work; the farmer is chatting over lunch.
jokes.punchline: The farmer casually mentions finding Native American artifacts in his pigpen as if this is an unremarkable detail of daily farm life — delivered with the same flat tone as everything else.
jokes.explanation: Minor atmospheric joke — the deadpan mention of arrowheads in the pigpen is part of the film's rural Idaho texture. Mildly funny as background absurdism but not a standout moment.

jokes.text: Napoleon forced to eat an unappetizing farm lunch — reaction shot as he faces whatever is on the plate at the farm.
jokes.setup: The farmer invites Napoleon to 'dig in' after a day of farm labor.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's 'Ew!' (at 41:32) suggests the farm food is visually revolting — the gap between the farmer's hospitality and the disgusting meal is a visual comedy beat, amplified by Napoleon's earlier 'Ew!' reaction.
jokes.explanation: Visual gag inferred from the 'Ew!' at 41:32 and the 'Well, dig in' at 41:54 — the farm lunch is apparently disgusting. Standard gross-out beat but consistent with the film's texture of mundane unpleasantness.

jokes.text: Can't find my checkbook. Hope you don't mind I pay you in change. — Six dollars. — That's, like, a dollar an hour.
jokes.setup: Napoleon has worked all day at the farm moving 8,000 chickens.
jokes.punchline: His entire day's wages are $6 in change — roughly a dollar an hour — and his response is not outrage but a deadpan accounting of the hourly rate, as if doing the math is the appropriate response to being exploited.
jokes.explanation: Napoleon's flat wage calculation — 'That's, like, a dollar an hour' — without any subsequent anger or protest is a perfect deadpan response to exploitation. His acceptance of the payment in change is also implied, deepening the pathetic comedy. Well-structured payoff to the entire farm work sequence.

jokes.text: Hi. Is Napoleon there? — Yes. — Can I talk to him? — You already are.
jokes.setup: Trisha calls Napoleon's house; he answers the phone.
jokes.punchline: When Trisha asks to speak to Napoleon, he responds 'You already are' — technically correct but socially tone-deaf, as normal phone etiquette would be to say 'This is Napoleon' or 'Speaking.'
jokes.explanation: 'You already are' is a perfect Napoleon-ism — technically correct, socially unaware, and delivered as if she should have known. The setup with two separate confirmation beats ('Is Napoleon there? — Yes. — Can I talk to him?') makes the punchline land with good rhythm.

jokes.text: It took me, like, three hours to finish the shading on your upper lip. It's probably the best drawing I've ever done.
jokes.setup: Trisha thanks Napoleon for the beautiful drawing he made of her; he responds with what he intends as a compliment.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon shares that he spent three hours shading her upper lip — an intimate and unflattering focus — and declares it his best work, oblivious to how this reads to the person with the notable upper lip.
jokes.explanation: Among the reel's very best jokes. 'Three hours to finish the shading on your upper lip' is a devastating line — Napoleon intends it as a compliment about his dedication, but it simultaneously implies the girl has a very pronounced upper lip AND that he found it worthy of three hours of artistic attention. 'It's probably the best drawing I've ever done' — said to the portrait subject — is the perfect cap. The cringe is total: he is simultaneously insulting her and complimenting himself, with zero awareness of either. Only Napoleon could deliver this. The gap between his intention and the actual content is the film's signature comedic gap.

jokes.text: Yeah, it's really... nice. — Yeah, well, I'll probably pick you up at 6:00 for the dance.
jokes.setup: Trisha has just been told Napoleon spent three hours shading her upper lip.
jokes.punchline: Trisha's halting '...nice' is a masterclass in polite discomfort — the pause before 'nice' contains all her conflicted feelings — and Napoleon's immediate pivot to logistics ('I'll probably pick you up at 6:00') shows he has no idea anything is wrong.
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat of Trisha's 'Yeah, it's really... nice' is the perfect straight-woman response — she can't be rude because he just asked her to the dance, but she can't pretend the upper-lip comment didn't happen. The ellipsis is doing real comedy work. Napoleon's instant logistics pivot reinforces his social blindness.

jokes.text: Who was that? — Trisha. — Who's she? — My woman I'm takin' to the dance. — You draw her a picture? — Heck, yes, I did!
jokes.setup: Napoleon hangs up with Trisha; Kip asks who called.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's designation of Trisha as 'my woman' — after a single phone call confirming a school dance — escalates his territorial language from 'my girlfriend's house' to even more possessive, delivered with the same flat certainty.
jokes.explanation: 'My woman' is a funny escalation from 'my girlfriend' — Napoleon's possessive vocabulary is running ahead of his actual relationship status. 'Heck, yes, I did!' as a response to drawing her a picture has good energy.

jokes.text: Just, like, a silk shirt or something. What are you gonna wear? — Deb has something for me. But you should probably get a suit.
jokes.setup: Napoleon and Pedro discuss what to wear to the school dance.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's plan is 'just, like, a silk shirt or something' — delivered with the casual confidence of a man who considers this sufficient formal attire — while Pedro mentions Deb has something for him, implying a more considered approach.
jokes.explanation: Minor fashion-discussion joke. Napoleon's silk shirt plan is consistent with his aesthetic sensibility but not an especially sharp joke on its own.

jokes.text: Pedro, how do you feel about that one? — It looks nice. — Yeah. It looks pretty sweet. It looks awesome. That suit, it's— It's incredible.
jokes.setup: Pedro is apparently trying on a suit for the dance, with Napoleon and others offering feedback.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's escalating praise — nice → pretty sweet → awesome → incredible — applied to what is likely a comically ill-fitting suit, delivered with zero irony, is a classic deadpan escalation. Pedro's flat 'It looks nice' is the straight-man anchor.
jokes.explanation: Napoleon's vocabulary escalation from 'nice' to 'incredible' in four beats is good structural comedy. The visual of whatever Pedro is wearing makes this a rewatch bonus — the suit is likely absurd and Napoleon's total sincerity about it being 'incredible' is perfect.

jokes.text: Can't you take me and then drop me off when you're done or whatever?
jokes.setup: Napoleon needs Uncle Rico to drive him to pick up Trisha for the dance; Uncle Rico has a sales call.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's request treats the school dance as equivalent in priority to Uncle Rico's business — 'or whatever' appended to what is for Napoleon an urgent situation reveals his studied casualness about things he actually cares about.
jokes.explanation: Minor character beat. Napoleon's 'or whatever' is consistent with his verbal affect but not especially funny on its own.

jokes.text: Well, I'll be back in a minute. Don't disturb me while I'm in there.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico needs to stop somewhere before taking Napoleon to pick up Trisha.
jokes.punchline: His instruction 'Don't disturb me while I'm in there' implies a private or significant errand, the specificity of which is left to the imagination — the mystery of what Uncle Rico is doing that requires such privacy is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Mild setup for an unseen beat. The portentous 'Don't disturb me while I'm in there' applied to whatever Uncle Rico is doing is minor character comedy — his self-importance extended to mundane activities.

jokes.text: Hi. I got your 24-piece set right here. [Uncle Rico at a door as Napoleon waits in van for his dance date pickup]
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico has told Napoleon he'll be 'back in a minute' and not to disturb him.
jokes.punchline: The 'minute' has stretched into Napoleon waiting while Uncle Rico makes a full sales pitch — the closing scene of the reel reveals Uncle Rico prioritized a sales call over Napoleon's dance date, treating them as equivalent.
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff to the reel's closing — Uncle Rico's greed/obliviousness causing Napoleon to miss his dance date pickup window is an earned comedic consequence. The reel ends on Uncle Rico at a door selling bowls while Napoleon waits, which is a tidy encapsulation of their dynamic.

jokes.text: Simón.
jokes.setup: Napoleon asks if Pedro's cousins are the ones with 'all the sweet hookups,' building up the cousins as cool, capable figures.
jokes.punchline: The cousin confirms with a single deadpan 'Simón' (Spanish slang for 'yes'), deflating any further explanation into one cool syllable.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — one word does all the work. The cultural contrast between Napoleon's nerdy Idaho vernacular ('sweet hookups') and the cousin's cool bilingual slang is the entire joke. Character-specific and effortless.

jokes.text: That's my ride.
jokes.setup: Trisha asks 'Who's that in my driveway?' with concern, implying she expects something impressive or alarming.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon flatly declares 'That's my ride' — implying his 'ride' to the dance is something embarrassingly humble (inferred to be a limo driven by Pedro's cousins, which is funny because it's unexpectedly extravagant, or alternately a beat-up car).
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the 'sweet hookups' setup — Pedro's cousins delivering Napoleon to the dance in style. Napoleon's flat, unimpressed delivery of 'That's my ride' as if it's nothing is perfect character economy.

jokes.text: Do you wanna go over by my friend Pedro and dance really quick?
jokes.setup: Napoleon is at the school dance. 'Forever Young' is playing. He needs to ask a girl to dance.
jokes.punchline: 'Dance really quick' — the qualifier 'really quick' is Napoleon's anxious, low-commitment way of asking, as if he's pre-negotiating an escape route from his own date invitation. It's socially maladroit in a deeply specific way.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Napoleon lines in the reel. 'Really quick' is doing enormous character work — it's his defense mechanism, his social anxiety, and his obliviousness all in one phrase. Only Napoleon Dynamite would hedge a dance invitation this way. High character integration and genuine originality.

jokes.text: If you can't find Trisha, I'll let you dance with Deb for a few songs.
jokes.setup: Napoleon is looking for his date Trisha at the dance.
jokes.punchline: He casually offers Deb as a consolation prize — framing her as a favor he's doing rather than something anyone would want. The oblivious generosity is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Napoleon's complete social obliviousness shines here — offering someone else's potential dance partner as a charitable gesture, delivered with zero self-awareness. Well-integrated into his character.

jokes.text: I like your sleeves. They're real big.
jokes.setup: Napoleon approaches Deb at the dance, presumably trying to make conversation or compliment her.
jokes.punchline: His idea of a compliment is 'I like your sleeves. They're real big.' — specific, sincere, and deeply uncool. The earnestness makes it funnier than any ironic compliment could be.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film. The specificity is what makes it extraordinary — not 'I like your outfit' but the sleeves, and not 'big' in a flattering way but as a pure observation. It's completely sincere, which makes it both sweet and hilarious. Only Napoleon could deliver this with zero irony. Earns its 8+ score: it became a cultural reference point for the film's particular brand of earnest awkwardness.

jokes.text: Thank you. I made them myself.
jokes.setup: Napoleon has just told Deb he likes her sleeves because they're 'real big.'
jokes.punchline: Deb accepts the bizarre compliment with complete sincerity and reveals she made the sleeves herself — validating the absurdity by owning it.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the sleeve joke. Deb's pride in her homemade oversized sleeves escalates the absurdity and makes both characters endearing weirdos together. The economy is excellent — four words close the joke.

jokes.text: How your glamour shots been going lately?
jokes.setup: Napoleon is trying to make conversation with Deb; glamour shots were previously established as Deb's side hustle
jokes.punchline: Napoleon treats 'glamour shots' as a totally normal professional pursuit to inquire about, with the casual tone of someone asking how business is going
jokes.explanation: The callback to Deb's entrepreneurial side hustle adds texture. Napoleon asking about it like a professional courtesy ('how's business?') is funny because it treats the most awkward possible topic as completely natural small talk.

jokes.text: Like, what are my skills? / Well, you have a sweet bike, and you're really good at hookin' up with chicks.
jokes.setup: Pedro asks Napoleon whether people will vote for him — genuinely uncertain about his own qualifications for class president.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's earnest campaign assessment: 'sweet bike' and 'hookin' up with chicks' — delivered as legitimate presidential qualifications with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Napoleon as political strategist is a great comic conceit. 'Sweet bike' as a campaign credential is perfectly absurd yet internally consistent with the film's Idaho teen logic. The character integration is strong — only Napoleon would assess a presidential campaign this way.

jokes.text: Plus you're, like, the only guy at school who has a mustache.
jokes.setup: Napoleon is listing Pedro's presidential qualifications.
jokes.punchline: Pedro's mustache — a physical trait and running visual gag — is presented as a serious electoral advantage.
jokes.explanation: The mustache as a campaign asset is a beautiful piece of absurdist logic. It's consistent with the film's world where normal social hierarchies are scrambled. Napoleon says it with complete conviction.

jokes.text: If I win, you can be my secretary or something.
jokes.setup: Napoleon offers to use all his skills for Pedro's campaign.
jokes.punchline: Pedro's flat, almost insulting reward offer — 'secretary or something' — delivered with zero ceremony, as if he barely thought about it.
jokes.explanation: Pedro's deadpan is perfectly deployed. Napoleon offered his full range of skills and Pedro responds with 'secretary or something' — the casual diminishment is very funny, and Pedro's flat affect makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Sweet! Plus I could be your bodyguard too. Or, like, Secret Service captain or... whatever.
jokes.setup: Pedro offers Napoleon the role of 'secretary or something' as a reward for helping with the campaign.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon enthusiastically accepts and immediately escalates himself from secretary to bodyguard to 'Secret Service captain' — an absurd self-promotion ladder delivered with total earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Napoleon's rapid self-promotion from secretary to 'Secret Service captain or whatever' is a great escalation beat. The 'or whatever' deflation at the end is perfect — he builds himself up and then immediately second-guesses it. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: It's a time machine, Napoleon. He bought it online.
jokes.setup: Napoleon and Kip find a strange device belonging to Uncle Rico. Napoleon asks what it's for.
jokes.punchline: Kip delivers 'It's a time machine, Napoleon. He bought it online.' with complete flat sincerity — as if buying a time machine online is a totally mundane transaction.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the film. The joke operates on multiple levels: Uncle Rico's delusional nostalgia, the absurdity of an online time machine purchase, and Kip's complete deadpan sincerity. 'He bought it online' is the perfect button — it treats the impossible as an ordinary consumer decision. Earns its 8+ score: genuinely quotable, perfectly structured, and entirely character-specific.

jokes.text: Yeah, right. It works, Napoleon. You don't even know.
jokes.setup: Napoleon expresses skepticism about the time machine.
jokes.punchline: Kip doubles down — 'It works, Napoleon. You don't even know.' — defending a mail-order time machine with the conviction of someone who has fully bought in.
jokes.explanation: 'You don't even know' as a defense of a time machine is perfect Kip. He's the credulous older brother who believes in internet miracles. The escalating commitment to the absurd premise is very funny.

jokes.text: Kill— the pow— Kill— / Turn it off! Turn it off!
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico and Kip attempt to activate the time machine. They've built up genuine anticipation.
jokes.punchline: The machine clearly malfunctions violently and immediately — their panicked 'Turn it off! Turn it off!' reveals the device is dangerous or at least terrifying rather than functional.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the time machine buildup. The abrupt escalation from hopeful activation to panicked shutdown is well-paced. The visual comedy of whatever the machine does to them (inferred from the panic) is the core laugh.

jokes.text: It's a piece of rap. It doesn't work. / Well, I could've told you that.
jokes.setup: The time machine has just failed spectacularly.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's flat dismissal ('piece of rap') and the deadpan 'Well, I could've told you that' — total anti-climax after the buildup.
jokes.explanation: Napoleon's 'piece of rap' (a minced oath, his version of 'piece of crap') is good character voice. The 'could've told you that' response is a classic deadpan button. Together they deflate the time machine fantasy efficiently.

jokes.text: I said the 12 pack, not the 24 pack. / You're just gonna have to mix and match. / Shut up. Say it so the whole world can hear.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico and Kip are arguing — apparently about breast enhancement product samples they're selling door to door.
jokes.punchline: The domestic squabbling over sample packs, combined with 'Say it so the whole world can hear,' reveals the absurdity of their MLM operation through petty argument.
jokes.explanation: The petty logistics argument over sample packs is funny because it treats an absurd product with mundane bickering. 'Say it so the whole world can hear' is good frustrated energy. Functional cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Napoleon, you know we can't afford the fun pack. You think money grows on trees in this family? Take it back. Get some Pampers for you and your brother while you're at it.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is arguing about product samples with Napoleon nearby.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Rico suddenly turns on Napoleon with a stream of domestic grievances — 'fun pack,' 'money grows on trees,' 'get some Pampers' — treating adult Napoleon and Kip like scolded children in a grocery store.
jokes.explanation: Uncle Rico's parental authority mode is funny because he has none — he's a freeloading uncle, not a parent. 'Get some Pampers for you and your brother' is a good specific insult that escalates the absurdity of his self-appointed guardianship.

jokes.text: The defect in that one is bleach. / That's correct. Yes!
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico and Kip appear to be testing or quizzing each other on their breast enhancement product's defects.
jokes.punchline: Kip celebrates identifying 'bleach' as a defect with 'That's correct. Yes!' — as if passing a product knowledge quiz is a genuine achievement worth celebrating.
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of enthusiastically studying a dubious MLM product — and celebrating correct answers about bleach defects — is good low-key comedy. Kip's genuine excitement is the key ingredient.

jokes.text: This tastes like the cow got into an onion patch.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico and Kip appear to be taste-testing milk samples as part of their sales preparation.
jokes.punchline: 'This tastes like the cow got into an onion patch' — a hyper-specific rural Idaho folk simile delivered with casual authority.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. The specificity of 'got into an onion patch' is precisely the kind of authentic rural Idaho vernacular that makes this film distinctive. It's not trying to be funny — it's just deeply specific and regional in a way that's genuinely original. High character integration: only someone from Uncle Rico's world would reach for this metaphor. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: They're pretty good except for one little problem. That little guy right there, he has nipple number five. A good dairy cow should have, like, four.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is evaluating dairy products/cows as part of his sales pitch preparation.
jokes.punchline: 'Nipple number five' — delivered with the gravity of a livestock expert identifying a serious defect, then explained with 'a good dairy cow should have, like, four.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. The escalation from 'one little problem' to 'nipple number five' is a perfect misdirection-to-absurd-reveal. The technical specificity ('a good dairy cow should have, like, four') delivered with deadpan expertise makes it funnier. It's unexpected, specific, and entirely rooted in this Idaho world. The 'like' in the middle of livestock expertise is a beautiful touch. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Do you think it's kinda warm in here? / No. / I think it's— They have the heater on or something. It seems pretty good to me. / You don't feel like your head is burning or— or anything? / No.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is campaigning for Summer Wheatly, handing out buttons. He starts complaining about being hot.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Rico's increasingly specific complaints about his head burning, while everyone around him is fine, foreshadows that something is wrong with him (a side effect of the breast enhancement product he's been sampling).
jokes.explanation: Setup comedy — the audience suspects the product he's been handling/sampling is causing side effects. The deadpan responses from others ('seems pretty good to me') while Rico escalates the symptoms is a good slow-burn cringe beat.

jokes.text: I'm gonna go home and lay down.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico has been complaining about his head burning during a campaign event.
jokes.punchline: He simply announces he's going home to lay down — abandoning the campaign event without ceremony, as if his breast-enhancement-product side effects are a mild inconvenience.
jokes.explanation: A quiet button to the burning head sequence. Works mainly as a setup-completion rather than a standalone joke, but the matter-of-fact delivery of illness mid-campaign is consistent with the film's deadpan tone.

jokes.text: Vote for Summer. Yeah, right. I'm not votin' for her. Then who are you gonna vote for? I'm votin' for Pedro Sanchez. Who do you think?
jokes.setup: Summer's campaign is canvassing the hallway. Napoleon is nearby.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's 'I'm votin' for Pedro Sanchez. Who do you think?' — delivered with exasperated obviousness, as if anyone asking otherwise is being ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: 'Who do you think?' as a tag is good Napoleon character voice — his loyalty to Pedro combined with his inability to understand why anyone would ask is a nice small moment.

jokes.text: So, that guy in Florida give you your money back yet? / Oh, I wrote him an e-mail, sayin' I'm gonna contact the authorities if I don't get a refund in full.
jokes.setup: Kip got scammed by an online seller (presumably related to the time machine purchase).
jokes.punchline: Kip's 'I wrote him an e-mail saying I'm gonna contact the authorities' — the threat is comically toothless and bureaucratic for someone who bought a fake time machine online.
jokes.explanation: Kip's very 2004 approach to consumer grievances — a threatening e-mail — is funny in context. The gap between the sci-fi absurdity of the purchase and the mundane legal threat is a good comic contrast.

jokes.text: Don't you ever wish you could go back with all the knowledge you have now? / I guess so. / Well, I'll tell you somethin' right now. You'd find your soul mate.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is waxing philosophical about going back in time — his obsession with 1982.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Rico pivots from general philosophical musing to telling Kip specifically that HE would 'find your soul mate' — implying Kip currently has no soul mate and is romantically hopeless.
jokes.explanation: The setup is Uncle Rico's standard time-travel fantasy, but the punchline's target — implying Kip is romantically doomed — is a small passive insult. Gets more rewatchable with knowledge of the Lafawnduh payoff coming minutes later.

jokes.text: I've already got a soul mate. / Oh, yeah. What's her name again? / Lafawnduh.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico implies Kip needs to go back in time to find a soul mate.
jokes.punchline: Kip reveals he already has one — 'Lafawnduh' — the name landing as an absurdist joke in itself, exotic and completely unexpected in rural Idaho.
jokes.explanation: The name 'Lafawnduh' is doing significant comedic work — it's both a beautiful and absurd name in the context of this Idaho world. Uncle Rico's 'Oh, yeah. What's her name again?' implies he's heard it before and can't quite process it. The reveal lands with genuine surprise and warmth. Strong setup/punchline structure.

jokes.text: She's flyin' out from Detroit for a few days.
jokes.setup: Kip has revealed his soul mate Lafawnduh. Uncle Rico is skeptical.
jokes.punchline: Detroit — the geographic and cultural distance from rural Idaho is the entire joke. Lafawnduh coming from Detroit to this tiny town for Kip is quietly absurd.
jokes.explanation: Detroit as the origin point for Kip's internet romance is a sharp geographic gag — maximum cultural distance from Idaho. The matter-of-fact delivery makes it funnier than any joke about it could be.

jokes.text: Why don't you sell some to that girlfriend of yours? You might as well do somethin' while you're doin' nothin'. / Because she doesn't need any. That's why.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico suggests Kip sell their breast enhancement products to Lafawnduh during her visit.
jokes.punchline: Kip's defensive 'Because she doesn't need any. That's why.' — a protective non-answer that also implies he's thought about this and is loyally defending his girlfriend's physique.
jokes.explanation: The indignant specificity of 'Because she doesn't need any. That's why.' — Kip is somehow both gallant and oblivious. It lands well because Kip is defending Lafawnduh before we've even met her, and his loyalty is oddly sweet and funny.

jokes.text: Hey. I did some drawings for the flyers.
jokes.setup: Napoleon shows up to help Pedro's campaign with flyer artwork.
jokes.punchline: The implied visual: Napoleon's campaign artwork is presumably his signature style of crude, earnest fantasy drawings (like the liger). The reveal of the drawings is the comedic beat.
jokes.explanation: Setup beat more than a full joke — the drawings themselves are the punchline, which the transcript can only infer. Works as character comedy because Napoleon's earnest artistic contribution to a political campaign is very him.

jokes.text: Why do you got your hood on like that? / Well, when I came home from school, my head started to get really hot. So I drank some cold water, but it didn't do nothing. So I laid in the bathtub for a while, but then I realized that it was my hair that was making my head so hot. So I went into my kitchen, and I shaved it all off.
jokes.setup: Pedro shows up wearing his hood pulled tight over his face. Napoleon asks why.
jokes.punchline: Pedro's completely logical, step-by-step explanation of why he shaved his head — delivered as a rational problem-solving sequence — is the joke. The logic is impeccable and totally absurd.
jokes.explanation: One of the best comedic monologues in the film. Pedro's methodical, deadpan elimination of solutions (cold water, bathtub) before arriving at shaving his head is perfect absurdist logic. The structure — 'I tried X but it didn't work, so I tried Y, but then I realized Z' — is impeccable. The specificity of 'I went into my kitchen and shaved it all off' as a matter-of-fact conclusion to medical problem-solving is excellent. Fully earns 8+.

jokes.text: I don't want anyone to see. / I know what you mean.
jokes.setup: Pedro has just revealed he shaved his head and doesn't want people to see.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's 'I know what you mean' — an utterly sincere expression of solidarity from someone who also feels socially invisible and embarrassed — is both funny and oddly touching.
jokes.explanation: Four words doing a lot of character work. Napoleon's 'I know what you mean' implies a whole inner life of social shame. It's both a funny deadpan response and a genuinely sweet moment of friendship. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: There's just so many options.
jokes.setup: Napoleon is apparently looking through wigs or hats to help Pedro cover his newly shaved head.
jokes.punchline: 'There's just so many options' — delivered with Napoleon's characteristic flat enthusiasm, as if selecting a disguise for his friend's shaved head is a pleasantly complex shopping problem.
jokes.explanation: Napoleon's flat delight at the array of options is a small but good character beat. The gap between the gravity of the situation (Pedro's social anxiety) and Napoleon's shopping-channel enthusiasm is the joke.

jokes.text: That one's good. Looks like a medieval warrior.
jokes.setup: Napoleon is evaluating head-covering options for Pedro.
jokes.punchline: 'Looks like a medieval warrior' — Napoleon's aesthetic framework for solving Pedro's social anxiety problem is entirely his own, rooted in his fantasy drawings and nerd obsessions.
jokes.explanation: 'Medieval warrior' as the standard of coolness Napoleon is shooting for is perfect character integration. Only Napoleon would evaluate a wig for a school campaign through the lens of medieval combat. Specific, funny, and entirely his voice.

jokes.text: You know, you're right. That's a good one.
jokes.setup: Napoleon has suggested a 'medieval warrior' option for Pedro's head.
jokes.punchline: Pedro's completely earnest 'You know, you're right. That's a good one.' — he genuinely agrees with the medieval warrior assessment with no irony.
jokes.explanation: Pedro's sincere agreement with Napoleon's absurd aesthetic judgment is the perfect button. His deadpan delivery of 'You know, you're right' as though Napoleon has made a genuinely insightful observation elevates both characters.

jokes.text: I think this matches your season, Pedro.
jokes.setup: Napoleon has been selecting a head covering for Pedro.
jokes.punchline: 'I think this matches your season, Pedro.' — Napoleon invoking color theory/seasonal palette analysis (a real aesthetic concept) completely sincerely while selecting a wig to hide a campaign-related head-shaving incident.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. Napoleon applying seasonal color theory to wig selection for his friend's involuntary head-shaving is a perfect collision of mundane beauty-parlor logic and completely absurd context. The specificity of 'matches your season' — a real but obscure concept — delivered with Napoleon's flat sincerity is genuinely original and very quotable. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Hey, give me 50 cents so I can buy a pop. / I don't have any, Randy. Come on. I'll pay you back. / I don't have— Stop. / Don't. Stop. Stop. / I'll do this to you. / Don't. Ow.
jokes.setup: A bully (Randy) demands 50 cents from Napoleon for a soda.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's 'I don't have any, Randy' — using the bully's first name as if they're on friendly terms mid-shakedown — plus the escalation to some kind of physical altercation ('I'll do this to you').
jokes.explanation: Napoleon using Randy's first name during a bullying incident is a small but good detail — it implies familiarity and total social confusion. The escalating stops and 'I'll do this to you' (some unspecified threat) is good physical comedy setup.

jokes.text: Hey, give me 50 cents so I can buy a pop. I don't have any, Randy. Come on. I'll pay you back. I don't have— Stop. Don't. Stop. Stop. — I'll do this to you. — Don't. Ow. — Here. Here.
jokes.setup: Randy asks Napoleon for 50 cents for a pop; Napoleon refuses
jokes.punchline: Randy physically coerces Napoleon — apparently an arm twist or similar — until Napoleon capitulates with 'Here. Here.' The escalation from casual request to physical extortion over fifty cents is the joke
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy and cringe — the escalation from request to coercion over 50 cents establishes the school's social hierarchy and Napoleon's low place in it. Functional but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: That's too bad.
jokes.setup: Napoleon has just been hurt by the bully Randy. Pedro asks 'How's your neck?'
jokes.punchline: Pedro's response to Napoleon's 'Stings' is simply 'That's too bad.' — delivered with zero urgency or additional comfort, as if Napoleon mentioned mild weather.
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfect economy, completely deadpan. Pedro's total lack of emotional escalation in response to his friend being hurt is funnier than any expression of concern would be. The flatness is the entire joke. High character integration — only Pedro delivers this.

jokes.text: Pedro offers you his protection.
jokes.setup: Napoleon has just been physically bullied by Randy. Pedro witnessed it.
jokes.punchline: Pedro offers 'protection' — framed in formal third person as if delivering a mob boss's terms — delivered completely flat, after doing nothing during the actual incident.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the entire film. The third-person declaration — 'Pedro offers you his protection' — is a perfect collision of mob movie formality, deadpan delivery, and complete absurdity (Pedro is not actually capable of providing any protection). The timing (after the incident is over) makes it even better. It's entirely original, deeply character-specific, structurally pristine, and maximally quotable. This is what 8.5+ looks like.

jokes.text: Hey, you Trisha? Yeah. You remember me? / I'm a friend of your mom's. I'm— I'm Napoleon's uncle. Uncle Rico.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico approaches Napoleon's date Trisha and introduces himself.
jokes.punchline: He introduces himself as 'a friend of your mom's' first — an adult trying to seem legitimate to a teenager — then corrects to 'Napoleon's uncle,' which is somehow worse, then says the name 'Uncle Rico' as if it explains everything.
jokes.explanation: Uncle Rico's social awkwardness with teenage girls is a great cringe beat. The stumbling self-introduction — friend of mom's, no wait, uncle — reveals his calculating but bungling nature. 'Uncle Rico' as a final identifier is funny because it sounds like a stage name.

jokes.text: Could you do me a favor? Could you give your mom a couple of these and tell 'em to hand 'em out to her friends or whoever? / You girls give me a call if you feel like you could use some.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico approached Napoleon's date under the guise of being a family friend — now he reveals his actual purpose: selling breast enhancement products to teenage girls via their mothers.
jokes.punchline: 'You girls give me a call if you feel like you could use some.' — the full cringe reveal. Uncle Rico is essentially implying to teenage girls that they may need breast enhancement products. Deeply inappropriate, delivered with zero self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of Uncle Rico's actual agenda — selling enhancement products to Napoleon's date — is a great cringe escalation. The specificity of 'you girls give me a call if you feel like you could use some' is the precise kind of oblivious inappropriateness that defines Uncle Rico as a character. Well-structured, character-specific, and genuinely uncomfortable in a funny way.

jokes.text: Why the heck you throwin' crap at my van, Napoleon?
jokes.setup: Napoleon has apparently been throwing things at Uncle Rico's van — an act of revenge the transcript skips over visually.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Rico's indignant 'Why the heck you throwin' crap at my van?' frames the confrontation around property damage, completely missing the actual grievance Napoleon has.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the confrontation. Uncle Rico prioritizing his van over any concern for what he did to Napoleon is consistent character work. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Everybody at school thinks I'm a freakin' idiot 'cause of you.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico sold breast enhancement products to Napoleon's date/classmates under Napoleon's name, ruining Napoleon's social reputation.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's accusation is funny because his social standing was already so low — the idea that this specific incident made everyone think he's an idiot, as opposed to his baseline behavior, is the ironic subtext.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on the irony that Napoleon's already at rock bottom socially, so 'everyone thinks I'm a freakin' idiot' implies a distinction that may not exist. It's more cringe-character territory than sharp comedy.

jokes.text: You're gonna clean my van... right now. / Get off of me, you 'bodaggit.'
jokes.setup: Napoleon confronts Uncle Rico about ruining his reputation.
jokes.punchline: 'Bodaggit' — Napoleon's invented/mangled profanity, delivered as his strongest available insult during a physical confrontation.
jokes.explanation: 'Bodaggit' is perfect Napoleon vocabulary — a minced oath that reveals his complete inability to actually swear. The fact that this is his angriest available insult during a genuine physical confrontation is both funny and oddly endearing. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Higher. No, no, higher. Yeah! Yeah. Hit it! Dang.
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is apparently having Kip throw a football to him — Uncle Rico's obsession with his 1982 football glory days.
jokes.punchline: The sequence of excited coaching ('Higher! Hit it!') followed by the deflated 'Dang.' suggests Rico failed to catch or make the play, undercutting his athlete self-image.
jokes.explanation: A callback to Uncle Rico's delusional athlete identity. The escalation to disappointment ('Dang.') is a small but satisfying payoff. Works better visually than it reads in transcript.

jokes.text: Look, Pedro. I don't know how they do things down in Juárez, but here in Idaho we have a little something called pride.
jokes.setup: Pedro is being reprimanded by a school official.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't know how they do things down in Juárez, but here in Idaho we have a little something called pride.' — the pompous Idaho chauvinism delivered in defense of... school election etiquette. The gap between the gravity of the speech and the pettiness of the offense is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The 'down in Juárez' line is a pointed satire of small-town provincial condescension. The official invoking Idaho 'pride' in the context of a middle school election is absurd in the best way. It's also quietly revealing about the film's social commentary without being preachy.

jokes.text: No. They just made me take down the flyers as a penalty for the piñatas.
jokes.setup: Napoleon asks Pedro if he's been disqualified from the race for the piñata incident.
jokes.punchline: 'As a penalty for the piñatas.' — Pedro's flat delivery of 'the piñatas' as a known category of offense, as if this is a routine election rule violation.
jokes.explanation: 'The piñatas' as a matter-of-fact consequence category is a great deadpan button to the whole piñata subplot. Pedro's flat acceptance of the penalty as a normal campaign development is perfect character work.

jokes.text: But we do it in Mexico all the time.
jokes.setup: The translator has just explained the rule against making piñatas of real people.
jokes.punchline: 'But we do it in Mexico all the time.' — Pedro's cousin offers this as a complete and sufficient counterargument, with zero awareness that it won't change anything.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the section. The cousin's complete sincerity and the total futility of the argument ('we do it in Mexico all the time' as a defense to an Idaho school official) is excellent. The economy is perfect — nine words that contain a whole cultural collision. High quotability.

jokes.text: Your hair looked great today.
jokes.setup: Pedro has been wearing a hood all day to hide his shaved head — an entire subplot about covering his hair loss.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon tells Pedro his hair 'looked great today' — either sincerely complimenting the wig/hood situation or genuinely unaware of the irony, both interpretations being equally funny.
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback button to the entire Pedro hair subplot. Napoleon's sincere compliment about hair that doesn't exist (or is a wig/hood) is exactly the kind of earnest, oblivious sweetness this film runs on. The economy is excellent and the callback structure is tight.

jokes.text: Who are you? / I'm Lafawnduh. / What are you doing here? / I'm waiting for Kip.
jokes.setup: Napoleon comes home to find a glamorous, stylish Black woman from Detroit sitting in his house.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm waiting for Kip.' — the visual and contextual contrast between Lafawnduh (the name, the look, the Detroit origin) and Kip (pale, awkward Idaho internet nerd) is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Lafawnduh buildup. The reveal works as both a visual gag (the contrast) and a character comedy beat. 'I'm waiting for Kip' as the punchline — presenting Kip as the natural conclusion — is well-timed and earns a genuine laugh.

jokes.text: Why are you so sweaty?
jokes.setup: Napoleon has just come home. Lafawnduh asks a direct, unfiltered question.
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's reply: 'I been practicing.' — 'Some dance moves.' The reveal that Napoleon has been secretly practicing dance is both a character revelation and a setup for the film's climax.
jokes.explanation: Lafawnduh's blunt 'Why are you so sweaty?' followed by Napoleon's matter-of-fact 'I been practicing / Some dance moves' is a great small exchange. Napoleon's secret dance practice is revealed casually, with no self-consciousness, which is perfect for the film's climax setup.

jokes.text: Sorry, Napoleon. We're just runnin' a little bit late for some prime rib.
jokes.setup: Kip arrives with Lafawnduh, looking transformed — apparently dressed up for a date.
jokes.punchline: 'Just runnin' a little bit late for some prime rib.' — Kip's casual announcement of a romantic dinner, delivered with his characteristic complete lack of affect, while standing in the rural Idaho house.
jokes.explanation: 'Prime rib' as Kip's romantic dinner destination is a good character-specific detail — aspirational in a specifically Idaho way. The casual delivery ('just runnin' a little bit late') normalizes the whole absurd situation.

jokes.text: Tell Uncle Rico not to wait up for me.
jokes.setup: Kip is heading out for a romantic prime rib dinner with Lafawnduh.
jokes.punchline: Kip asking Napoleon to tell Uncle Rico 'not to wait up' — as if he's a teenager telling his parent he'll be late — inverts the household dynamic (Rico is the adult, Kip is the grown man).
jokes.explanation: A small but good inversion beat. Kip treating Uncle Rico as a parental figure to report to ('don't wait up') while simultaneously showing more romantic success than Rico is good character irony.

jokes.text: Here. You might like that. My cousin made it.
jokes.setup: Kip is about to leave for his date. He pauses to hand Napoleon something.
jokes.punchline: He gives Napoleon what is implied to be a mix CD or cassette from his cousin — a random, unexplained gift on the way out the door, presented with zero context, as if this is a completely normal parting gesture.
jokes.explanation: Setup beat for what turns out to be a D-Qwon dance groove mixtape that fuels Napoleon's climactic dance. 'My cousin made it' as the entire sales pitch is a good low-key absurdist moment. Gets rewatch value from the payoff.

jokes.text: Lafawnduh is the best thing that has ever happened to me. I'm a hundred percent positive that she's my soul mate.
jokes.setup: Kip is apparently delivering this as a sincere declaration about Lafawnduh.
jokes.punchline: The gap between Kip's complete flatness of delivery and the magnitude of the claim ('the best thing that has ever happened to me') is the joke — maximum sincerity expressed with zero emotional register.
jokes.explanation: Kip's flat sincerity about Lafawnduh being his soul mate — delivered with the same affect as ordering a sandwich — is both funny and oddly moving. It's a callback payoff to the soul mate conversation earlier and a character moment for Kip. The 'hundred percent positive' is particularly good.

jokes.text: Napoleon, I'm sure there's a babe out there for you too.
jokes.setup: Kip has just declared Lafawnduh is the best thing that has ever happened to him.
jokes.punchline: He condescendingly reassures Napoleon that 'there's a babe out there for you too' — using 'babe' completely sincerely, while framing Napoleon as the romantically hopeless one, delivered flatly.
jokes.explanation: Kip offering Napoleon romantic hope — using the word 'babe' with complete sincerity — is a funny inversion. Kip, the previously hopeless internet dater, is now dispensing romantic wisdom to Napoleon. The flat delivery makes 'babe' land harder than it would with any affect.

jokes.text: Peace out.
jokes.setup: Kip is departing for his prime rib date with Lafawnduh, having just dispensed romantic advice to Napoleon.
jokes.punchline: 'Peace out.' — Kip's signing off with hip-hop slang, delivered in his flattest possible Idaho voice, is the button on his entire character arc of transformation via Lafawnduh.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable closing beats in the film. 'Peace out' in Kip's perfectly flat Idaho voice is a beautiful character moment — it shows how Lafawnduh has already begun reshaping him while also being deeply funny because of how wrong it sounds. Maximum economy (two words), maximum character integration, and it's become a cultural shorthand for the film. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Uncle Rico's creepy photo shoot setup: suggesting foam, billowy fabric, and a fan for Deb's portrait session
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is ostensibly helping Deb with a photography/glamour shoot, framing it as a professional service
jokes.punchline: His suggestions — pink sheets, foam wrapping, billowy fabric, a fan — escalate into unmistakably sleazy territory while he maintains a veneer of professionalism
jokes.explanation: Classic Uncle Rico: the comedy comes entirely from his delusional self-perception as a smooth operator. 'Billowy's good' as Napoleon's innocent suggestion made real in a creepy context is perfect. The escalation of soft-focus photography clichés (foam! tinsel! a fan!) reads as a parody of cheap glamour-shot studios but filtered through Rico's predatory obliviousness. High character integration because only Rico — a man-child trapped in 1982 — would genuinely think this was charming.

jokes.text: "You know, Deborah, you have... striking features."
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is supposedly running a professional photo shoot for Deb
jokes.punchline: He pivots to a creepy, unsolicited personal compliment delivered with exaggerated sincerity, dropping 'Deborah' like a used-car salesman going for the close
jokes.explanation: The formal use of 'Deborah' instead of 'Deb' is a small but perfect detail — Rico treating a teenage girl like a conquest. The ellipsis-laden delivery ('you have... striking features') apes the cadence of a Hallmark villain. Economy is high: five words do enormous comedic work by implying a vast iceberg of Rico's delusion.

jokes.text: "Such a soft face should be complimented with a... soft body."
jokes.setup: Rico has just called Deb's face soft and striking — seemingly building toward a photographic tip
jokes.punchline: The punchline pivots to 'soft body' — a thinly veiled pitch for the herbal bust-enhancement product, but delivered with the cadence of a creep hitting on a teenager
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke of the Rico-Deb sequence. The structure is elegant: 'soft face… soft body' uses repetition as a bait-and-switch. The audience anticipates a photography term; instead Rico is essentially negging a teenager into buying a fake product. The long pause before 'soft body' sells it as a dramatic reveal. It's deeply uncomfortable and completely in character.

jokes.text: "My friends and clients, they call me 'Uncle Rico.'"
jokes.setup: Deb addresses him as 'Mr. Rico' in a moment of alarm, trying to establish a formal boundary
jokes.punchline: Rico rebrands himself as 'Uncle Rico' — a nickname that sounds warm and familial coming from a stranger making unwanted advances on a teenage girl, making it more unsettling, not less
jokes.explanation: Possibly the most character-specific line in this reel. 'Uncle Rico' as a self-applied nickname is inherently funny — normal uncles don't introduce themselves that way. The fact that he's solicited this nickname from 'friends and clients' implies a whole sad ecosystem of people who've adopted his mythology. It's also a callback to his established character from earlier reels. High character integration score because this line IS the character.

jokes.text: Deb, alarmed: 'What are you doing?' — Rico: 'Shh. Don't say another word.'
jokes.setup: It becomes clear that whatever Rico is doing in the photoshoot setup has escalated to a point that frightens Deb
jokes.punchline: 'Shh. Don't say another word.' — Rico's response is not reassurance but a command. The shushing makes everything worse by implying he's in a romantic headspace.
jokes.explanation: Four words do enormous work. 'Shh' is the wrong response to someone asking what you're doing. The audience's imagination fills in the visual. Economy is near-perfect: shorter and funnier than any longer version.

jokes.text: "Napoleon told me you'd be interested."
jokes.setup: Deb is visibly alarmed by Rico's advances; he needs to justify his presence
jokes.punchline: Rico invokes Napoleon as the matchmaker for this encounter, implying Napoleon set Deb up for the creepy sales pitch — which is simultaneously a betrayal revelation and an absurd excuse
jokes.explanation: This line serves double duty: it's a plot bomb (setting up Deb's anger at Napoleon) and a character joke (Rico is so oblivious he thinks invoking Napoleon's name is reassuring). The comedy comes from the audience processing the full chain of dysfunction this implies.

jokes.text: "You stop wishin', and call me when you're ready."
jokes.setup: Deb has presumably fled or recoiled from the shoot; Rico needs an exit line
jokes.punchline: Rico delivers a smooth-operator sign-off that belongs in a cheesy 1970s cologne ad, completely unbothered that the encounter went catastrophically wrong
jokes.explanation: The joke is Rico's total unawareness that he's been rejected. 'You stop wishin'' implies Deb is pining for him — a delusional inversion of reality. This is deadpan because it's delivered sincerely by a man who genuinely believes it. Strong economy: seven words sketch a complete portrait of his delusion.

jokes.text: Deb calls Napoleon to accuse him of setting her up, saying she 'doesn't need herbal enhancers to feel good about herself'
jokes.setup: Napoleon is completely blindsided — he had no idea Rico was pitching Deb the bust-enhancement product in his name
jokes.punchline: Deb's specific grievance — 'I don't need herbal enhancers to feel good about myself' — reveals the full humiliating scope of what Rico did, landing as both plot payoff and an absurdly specific complaint
jokes.explanation: The payoff works because we've been waiting to see the fallout of Rico's scheme. Deb's indignant specificity ('herbal enhancers') is funnier than a generic 'you're terrible' reaction. Napoleon's confused 'What?' is the perfect straight-man reaction — he's genuinely in the dark.

jokes.text: "And if you're so concerned about that, why don't you try eating some yourself?"
jokes.setup: Deb is furious at Napoleon for supposedly endorsing Rico's bust-enhancement pitch
jokes.punchline: She flips the insult back at Napoleon — suggesting he eat the breast-enhancement supplements — an absurd but perfectly spiteful comeback that doubles as an inadvertent gender-based burn
jokes.explanation: Sharp and spiteful in a way that's endearing for Deb. The structure is clean: her anger turns into an inadvertently absurd comeback. Telling an awkward teenage boy to eat breast-enhancement pills is specific enough to be genuinely funny rather than a generic insult. Good economy.

jokes.text: "She says she doesn't want you here when she gets back because you've been ruining everybody's lives and eatin' all our steak."
jokes.setup: Napoleon tells Uncle Rico that Grandma called and wants him gone — a serious domestic eviction
jokes.punchline: The list of grievances culminates in 'eatin' all our steak' — a mundane, petty complaint that deflates the drama and characterizes the household perfectly
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in this reel. The structure is classic: escalate to 'ruining everybody's lives' (big, dramatic) then immediately deflate with 'eatin' all our steak' (tiny, specific). The bathos is perfectly calibrated — the steak grievance is treated with equal moral weight to life-ruining. It's deeply Napoleon: he cares about the steak as much as the larger injustice. Highly quotable, strong economy, and completely character-specific. Approaches the 8-point anchor quality.

jokes.text: "Get off my property!" / "It's a free country. I can do whatever I want." / "Get off my property or I'll call the cops on you." / "Well, then do it. Go on." / "Maybe I will. Gosh!"
jokes.setup: Napoleon is trying to kick Uncle Rico off the property; Rico refuses to leave
jokes.punchline: The standoff devolves into a playground-level argument ('It's a free country') and Napoleon's threat to call the cops deflates into 'Maybe I will. Gosh!' — the least intimidating possible exit
jokes.explanation: Two man-children in a territorial dispute neither can win. 'It's a free country' from a grown adult is funny because Rico has regressed to grade-school logic. Napoleon's threat to call the cops followed by 'Maybe I will. Gosh!' perfectly captures his powerlessness. 'Gosh' as Napoleon's signature exclamation doing all the heavy lifting at the end.

jokes.text: "No, not unless she likes fish."
jokes.setup: Napoleon tells Pedro that Deb hates him now and asks Pedro if he has anything to give her as a peace offering
jokes.punchline: Pedro deadpans that he has nothing to give her 'unless she likes fish' — a completely literal, unhelpful response that reveals he has apparently just been fishing
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Pedro deadpan. The gap between the emotional weight of Napoleon's situation (his friendship is ruined) and Pedro's pragmatic, literal response (I have fish) is a perfect economy-of-absurdity joke. 'Unless she likes fish' is an unexpected qualifier that makes the joke. High economy score — six words, big laugh. Very Pedro-specific.

jokes.text: "Just tell 'em that their wildest dreams will come true if they vote for you."
jokes.setup: Pedro asks Napoleon what to say in his campaign speech; Napoleon is advising him as a political strategist
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's grand campaign advice is a maximally vague, hyperbolic promise — 'wildest dreams' — delivered with complete sincerity as if it's sage wisdom
jokes.explanation: This line sets up the later payoff when Pedro actually delivers it. As standalone advice from a teenager who has no idea what he's talking about, it's endearingly absurd — it sounds like a Miss America answer. The fact that Napoleon says it with total confidence elevates it. It becomes funnier in retrospect when Pedro delivers the line verbatim to the whole school. High quotability because the film made this a minor cultural touchstone.

jokes.text: "Dang it!" — Napoleon reacting to something off-screen, presumably a failed skill or mishap
jokes.setup: Scene transition; Napoleon is alone doing something (likely practicing a skill or attempting something for himself)
jokes.punchline: His signature exclamation of frustration, issued to no one, in the dark — the joke is the smallness and isolation of his private failures
jokes.explanation: 'Dang it' is a Napoleon signature — his impotent, mild profanity. Without visual context in the transcript, the comedy is partly inferential: we know Napoleon is probably doing something futile alone. The joke is primarily character-based and relies heavily on Jon Heder's delivery in the film. Lower craft scores because without the visual it's thin.

jokes.text: "After using Bust Must Plus, I have such big bosoms—" — Napoleon reads the product testimonial aloud before stopping
jokes.setup: Uncle Rico is showing Napoleon testimonials for the Bust Must Plus herbal supplement; he invites Napoleon to read one
jokes.punchline: Napoleon reads the testimonial — 'I have such big bosoms' — and abruptly stops, saying he doesn't feel comfortable reading it
jokes.explanation: The joke is Napoleon's oblivious discomfort — he'll say 'big bosoms' on camera without registering why that's weird, then suddenly feel 'uncomfortable' mid-sentence. The word 'bosoms' is inherently funny in Napoleon's flat Midwestern delivery. His belated moral qualm (stopping mid-testimonial) is the punchline.

jokes.text: "Oh, that's fine. That's fine. But do you feel comfortable with me?"
jokes.setup: Napoleon says he's not comfortable reading the breast-enhancement testimonial aloud
jokes.punchline: Rico pivots immediately to asking if Napoleon feels 'comfortable with me' — a completely non-sequitur reframe that sounds like a therapist, a predator, or a used-car salesman (all of which apply to Rico)
jokes.explanation: Rico's ability to redirect any discomfort back toward himself as a form of rapport-building is a perfect character trait. 'Do you feel comfortable with me?' in this context is profoundly inappropriate and also meaningless as a sales technique. The double 'that's fine' before the pivot apes the rhythm of a sleazy salesman absorbing an objection.

jokes.text: Rico gestures to a chart or diagram indicating where Napoleon could be physically, implying a breast size upgrade area
jokes.setup: Rico is trying to sell Napoleon on the bust-enhancement product by showing him a chart
jokes.punchline: Rico points to a location on the chart ('here') with the implication being where Napoleon's chest size could be — applying a product designed for women to an awkward teenage boy
jokes.explanation: Primarily a visual gag — the comedy is in what Rico is pointing to on the diagram. Without visuals this reads flat, but in context it's another layer of Rico's exploitation of Napoleon. The extended pause before 'here' (noted in the transcript with timestamps) suggests the visual IS the joke.

jokes.text: Summer promises 'two new pop machines,' 'a glitter Bonnebell dispenser for all the girls' bathrooms,' and 'new cheerleading uniforms' in her presidential speech
jokes.setup: Summer frames herself as a serious candidate who will improve the school for everyone
jokes.punchline: Her entire platform is nakedly self-serving: pop machines (teenage luxury), Bonnebell lip gloss for the girls' bathrooms (her specific demographic), and new cheerleading uniforms (her activity). The irony is she doesn't realize this is all for herself.
jokes.explanation: A solid satirical jab at student government politics — the specificity of 'glitter Bonnebell dispenser' elevates it above generic mean-girl caricature. The escalation from pop machines to cosmetics dispensers to uniforms is a nice structural arc. Works best as setup for the contrast with Pedro's bizarre-but-earnest speech.

jokes.text: "Who wants to eat 'chimini-changas' next year?"
jokes.setup: Summer is giving her class president speech, listing perks she'll deliver
jokes.punchline: She mispronounces 'chimichanga' as 'chimini-changa' with total confidence — a small but perfect character detail showing she's a popular girl who doesn't know what a chimichanga actually is
jokes.explanation: One small word does enormous work. 'Chimini-changa' is funnier than a full satirical speech about shallow student government promises because it's specific, earned, and completely character-driven. It implies a whole worldview: Summer is the girl who thinks chimichangas are exotic food she learned about from the Olive Garden. High character integration — this mistake could only come from Summer.

jokes.text: "Not me. See, with me, it will be summer all year long. Vote for Summer."
jokes.setup: Summer has asked who wants chimichangas and pivots to her closing argument
jokes.punchline: Her entire closing statement is a pun on her own name — 'it will be summer all year long' — which she delivers with complete earnestness, as if this is a serious campaign vision
jokes.explanation: The pun is groan-worthy in the best way — it's exactly the kind of slogan a popular-but-not-bright girl would think was brilliant. The character integration saves it from being just a bad pun; it IS Summer's character. The joke is that she thinks this is a mic drop.

jokes.text: "A skit? You perform a skit after your speech, Pedro." / "What? A flippin' skit? Why didn't anybody tell us about this?"
jokes.setup: Napoleon and Pedro are backstage watching Summer perform a polished skit with the Happy Hands Club; they had no idea a skit was required
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's panicked 'flippin' skit' and his baffled complaint that nobody told them — said while watching Summer perform a full choreographed number — is the joke. They are catastrophically unprepared.
jokes.explanation: 'A flippin' skit' is a perfect Napoleon exclamation — mild profanity, genuine outrage, completely impotent. The situation comedy here is strong: they're watching a full professional-level performance while realizing they have nothing prepared. The helpless comedy of the unaware is a classic structure, well executed.

jokes.text: "I don't want to be president anyway."
jokes.setup: Pedro and Napoleon are panicking backstage about having no skit; the situation seems hopeless
jokes.punchline: Pedro deadpans 'I don't want to be president anyway' — a complete, serene abandonment of the entire campaign premise, delivered as a sincere statement rather than a joke
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the film. It's perfectly Pedro: a complete non-sequitur that is also deeply honest. He genuinely doesn't care. The comedy is in the gap between how much everyone around him has invested in this campaign and Pedro's total detachment from his own goal. Maximum economy — five words that reveal the entire character. The deadpan delivery makes it land as a profound statement rather than self-pity. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in structural quality and exceeds it in character specificity.

jokes.text: "Pedro, just listen to your heart. That's what I do."
jokes.setup: Pedro is despairing; Napoleon offers advice
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's earnest advice — 'listen to your heart, that's what I do' — is ironically hilarious because Napoleon demonstrably does NOT listen to his heart in any conventional sense; his heart leads him to tater tots and fantasy sequences
jokes.explanation: Napoleon as motivational speaker is inherently funny given how socially dysfunctional he is. The sincerity with which he says 'that's what I do' — as if he's a paragon of emotional wisdom — is the joke. Works because of character irony.

jokes.text: Pedro's presidential speech: suggesting bringing 'holy santos' to guard the high school hallways and invoking 'El Santo Niño de Atocha' whose sighting was reported by 'my Aunt Concha'
jokes.setup: Pedro takes the stage to deliver his presidential speech; the audience expects a standard student-government pitch
jokes.punchline: Pedro sincerely proposes placing religious statues in the hallways for luck, cites a specific Catholic saint by full name, and vouches for the saint's power via his aunt's personal vision — delivered with complete earnestness as a school-improvement policy
jokes.explanation: One of the great absurdist comedy beats in the film. The specificity is everything: not just 'religious statues' but 'El Santo Niño de Atocha,' not just 'my aunt said she saw him' but 'my Aunt Concha has seen him.' The comedy operates on multiple levels: Pedro is completely sincere (not ironic), the proposal is genuinely bizarre as campaign policy, and yet it's weirdly moving because Pedro is being authentically himself. 'My Aunt Concha has seen him' is a perfect sentence. This is the kind of absurdist comedy that only works when you've built the character — it's entirely earned. Near the top of the reel in quality.

jokes.text: "If you vote for me, all of your wildest dreams will come true."
jokes.setup: Earlier, Napoleon advised Pedro to promise voters that 'their wildest dreams will come true'
jokes.punchline: Pedro delivers the line verbatim, with his characteristic flat affect, following the entirely sincere discussion of holy santos — the contrast between the supernatural sincerity and the vague campaign slogan is comic
jokes.explanation: The callback structure is perfect. Napoleon's advice — which sounded like absurd non-advice when he gave it — becomes Pedro's entire closing argument, delivered with complete deadpan sincerity. The joke has two layers: (1) it's a callback payoff, and (2) it works as a commentary on actual political rhetoric — the most meaningless possible campaign promise, stated as fact. The deadpan delivery by Pedro makes it funnier than any enthusiastic delivery could. This became the most quoted line from the film for a reason. High quotability.

jokes.text: Long pause before Napoleon's dance skit begins — the audience (and viewer) has no idea what Pedro's 'skit' will be
jokes.setup: The announcer says 'I hope you'll enjoy a skit by Pedro Sanchez'; the audience waits; Napoleon had no plan
jokes.punchline: The gap between the announcement and the music starting is an extended beat of pure anticipatory awkwardness — the audience has no idea what's coming
jokes.explanation: The long silence before the dance begins functions as comedy through pure tension. The film has established that they had no plan — so the silence is loaded with anticipatory dread. This is primarily a structural/timing joke that the transcript captures incompletely, but the timestamps suggest roughly a minute of silence/music before the dance begins.

jokes.text: MC announcement: 'Up next, I hope you'll enjoy a skit by Pedro Sanchez.' — followed by a 43-second silence/gap before music starts
jokes.setup: Pedro has no skit prepared; the MC cheerfully introduces one anyway
jokes.punchline: The gap between the MC's introduction and the music starting (over 40 seconds in film time) is the audience experiencing the same dread Pedro and Napoleon feel — silence before the unknown
jokes.explanation: The anticipatory dread is a real comedy tool, and in the film the gap presumably shows Pedro and Napoleon's faces before the music saves them. The joke is structural — setup (no skit prepared) + gap + unexpected music = relief laugh.

jokes.text: Napoleon performs a full solo dance routine to 'Canned Heat' by Jamiroquai as Pedro's campaign skit — a completely unexpected, earnest, technically skilled performance
jokes.setup: Napoleon and Pedro had no skit prepared; Pedro is about to lose the election; Napoleon told Pedro to 'listen to your heart'
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's solution is to perform an elaborate, committed solo dance routine — in moon boots, with full conviction — that is simultaneously terrible and incredible. The audience's reaction shifts from silence to applause.
jokes.explanation: The climactic joke of the entire film. It earns a 9+ because it is genuinely one of the most memorable comedic moments in 2000s American cinema — a cultural touchstone. The comedy operates on multiple simultaneous registers: (1) it's completely unexpected as a solution, (2) Napoleon's utter commitment is itself funny and moving, (3) the dance is simultaneously bad and good in a way that defies easy categorization, (4) it pays off every 'Napoleon has secret skills' thread from the whole film, (5) it works as physical comedy AND character comedy AND emotional payoff. The character integration score is 10/10 — no other character in any film could do exactly this dance in exactly this context. This is what a 9+ craft score looks like.

jokes.text: "I caught you a delicious bass."
jokes.setup: After the dance, the election results, and the climax of the film, Napoleon shows up — apparently to make peace with Deb
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's gesture of reconciliation is presenting Deb with a fish he caught — the most Napoleon-possible peace offering, delivered with complete sincerity ('delicious')
jokes.explanation: A magnificent callback payoff. Pedro said 'not unless she likes fish' as a throwaway joke; Napoleon took it literally and went fishing. The word 'delicious' is the kicker — it implies Napoleon has tasted it, or at minimum assessed its quality, as if this is a normal gift to bring someone. This is simultaneously one of the most earnest and funniest moments in the film. High on every dimension: original, perfectly structured as a callback, completely character-specific, economic, and entirely earned. Near the 8.5 anchor quality, arguably above it.

jokes.text: "You wanna play me?"
jokes.setup: Napoleon is making peace with Deb after all the drama; the emotional resolution is underway
jokes.punchline: Napoleon's follow-up offer is to play tetherball with Deb — an activity that is simultaneously childlike, innocent, and oddly perfect as a form of reconciliation for Napoleon
jokes.explanation: The final joke of the film (before the credits sequence). 'You wanna play me?' is perfect character comedy: Napoleon's version of 'will you be my friend/girlfriend?' is a tetherball challenge. It's innocent, dorky, completely sincere, and utterly Napoleon. The fact that this functions as the film's emotional resolution — through a tetherball invitation — is itself the joke and the heart. The scene then shows them playing, suggesting Deb accepts. High economy and character integration.

jokes.text: "Where the heck's Napoleon?" — Pedro asking at Kip's wedding while Napoleon is absent
jokes.setup: Kip's wedding is underway; the whole family is present
jokes.punchline: Napoleon is conspicuously absent from his own brother's wedding, and Pedro — himself an outsider to the family — is the one asking about him, suggesting Napoleon's absence is both rude and completely in character
jokes.explanation: A mild character beat — the joke is that Pedro notices Napoleon's absence before anyone else apparently does, and the response 'I don't know' implies everyone has accepted that Napoleon does unpredictable things. Functional but not strong.

jokes.text: "Lafawnduh Lucas, do you take Kipland Ronald Dynamite..."
jokes.setup: Kip's wedding ceremony begins; the officiant reads the formal vows
jokes.punchline: The formal recitation of 'Kipland Ronald Dynamite' as a legal name — combined with the contrast of this awkward, pale, online-dating-addicted man marrying the glamorous Lafawnduh — makes the name itself a joke
jokes.explanation: 'Kipland Ronald Dynamite' in a wedding ceremony is inherently absurd — the full legal name sounds both ridiculous and oddly dignified. The juxtaposition of this name with the gravity of the vows is the joke. Also mild wordplay in that 'Dynamite' as a surname sounds like a bad action movie character.

jokes.text: The name 'Kipland Ronald Dynamite' read formally at the wedding altar
jokes.setup: The officiant reads the groom's full legal name during the ceremony
jokes.punchline: 'Kipland Ronald Dynamite' — hearing the Dynamite family surname in a formal, solemn wedding context is inherently funny; 'Kipland' as a formal given name is an additional absurdist detail
jokes.explanation: 'Kipland Ronald Dynamite' in a formal ceremony is a good laugh. The contrast between the solemnity of a wedding and 'Dynamite' as a legal surname works on the same principle as 'Kipland' — both feel like names someone invented to be slightly absurd.

jokes.text: "You know I do."
jokes.setup: The officiant asks Kip if he takes Lafawnduh as his wife in the traditional wedding vow format
